ask: Which of the following does the availability goal of the CIA triad protect?

options.t: Data stays secret from unauthorized parties
options.why: Keeping data secret is confidentiality, a different leg of the triad.
Keeping data accurate and unchanged is integrity, a different leg of the triad.

options.t: Authorized users can reach data when needed
options.why: Availability keeps systems and data accessible to authorized users when they need them.

options.t: Senders cannot deny sending their data
options.why: That is non-repudiation, a separate concept and not one of the three legs.

explain: The triad has three goals: confidentiality keeps data secret, integrity keeps it accurate, and availability keeps it reachable for authorized users when needed.

ask: Which of the following pairs a CIA triad goal with a control that protects it?

options.why: Hashing detects any change to data, which protects integrity.
Redundant servers keep a service running, which protects availability, not secrecy.
Encryption keeps data secret, which protects confidentiality, not access.
Fault tolerance keeps systems running through failures, which protects availability.

explain: Encryption and access controls serve confidentiality; hashing and digital signatures serve integrity; redundancy and fault tolerance serve availability.

stem: A records manager at a county court must be able to detect whether anyone alters a stored judgment file, even an employee with valid permission to open it.
ask: Which of the following controls meets this requirement?

options.why: Fault tolerance keeps systems running through failures; it does not detect changes.
Redundant servers keep the file reachable; they do not detect changes.
Access controls limit who can open the file, but the stem includes employees who already have permission.
A stored hash no longer matches once the file changes, so any alteration is detected.

detail: detect whether anyone alters a stored judgment file
explain: Detecting change is the integrity goal, and hashing is the integrity control that shows when data has been altered.

stem: A help desk lead at an online retailer must keep the order site running if one web server fails during a holiday sale.
ask: Which of the following controls supports this requirement?

options.why: Hashing detects changes to data; it does nothing when a server fails.
A second server takes over when one fails, which keeps the site available.
Encryption keeps data secret; it does not keep the site running.
Signatures prove data is unchanged and who signed it; they do not keep a service up.

detail: if one web server fails
explain: Keeping the site reachable through a failure is availability, which redundancy protects.

stem: A pharmacist at a pharmacy chain finds that an intruder edited the dosage values in several stored prescriptions. No prescriptions were copied out, and the system stayed online.
ask: Which of the following security goals did the intruder harm?

options.why: Nothing was disclosed; the stem says no prescriptions were copied out.
Unauthorized changes to stored data harm integrity.
The system stayed online, so access was not lost.
No one is denying having sent or signed something; the harm is that records were changed.

detail: edited the dosage values in several stored prescriptions
explain: The data was changed without authorization while it stayed secret and reachable, so integrity was harmed.

stem: An HR manager at a staffing agency learns that a spreadsheet of employee salaries was emailed to an outside personal account. The file was not changed, and every system stayed up.
ask: Which of the following security goals was harmed?

options.why: The stem says the file was not changed.
Every system stayed up, so access was not lost.
Accounting is the AAA function that records what users did, not a goal of the triad; the harm here is that data was disclosed.
Salary data reached someone not authorized to see it, which harms confidentiality.

detail: emailed to an outside personal account
explain: A disclosure to an unauthorized party is a confidentiality breach, even when the data itself is untouched.

stem: A site reliability engineer at a concert ticket seller watches the event page time out for every buyer while hijacked devices around the world flood it with requests. No data was viewed or modified.
ask: Which of the following security goals did this attack target?

options.why: A flood that stops the site from answering is a DDoS attack on availability.
No data was read, so nothing was disclosed.
No data was altered.
No sender is denying an action; the site simply stopped answering.

detail: time out for every buyer
explain: A distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack floods a service from many devices so authorized users cannot reach it, which targets availability.

stem: A database administrator at a law firm must make sure that client files copied from a stolen backup drive cannot be read by the thief.
ask: Which of the following controls meets this requirement?

options.why: A hash detects changes, but the files themselves stay readable.
A signature proves who signed and that nothing changed; it does not hide the contents.
Encrypted files are unreadable without the key, so a thief who copies them cannot read them.
More copies help availability and give a thief nothing less to read.

detail: cannot be read by the thief
explain: Keeping data secret from unauthorized people is confidentiality, and encryption is its main control.

stem: A security analyst at a regional hospital reviews the incident queue below.
ask: Which of the following security goals did TKT-2052 harm?

lines: TKT-2041  Price table on the web shop changed by an unknown account
TKT-2047  Patient list posted on a public file share
TKT-2052  Ticketing system offline after its only disk failed
TKT-2058  Visitor log printed and left in the lobby

options.why: That fits TKT-2041, where data was changed; TKT-2052 changed nothing.
That fits TKT-2047 and TKT-2058, where data was exposed; TKT-2052 exposed nothing.
No one in TKT-2052 is denying an action; a system went offline.
TKT-2052 is a system that cannot be reached after a failure, which harms availability.

detail: Ticketing system offline after its only disk failed
explain: An outage harms availability. A single disk with no redundancy is why one failure took the system offline.

stem: A compliance officer at a credit union must be able to detect any change made to stored loan records.
ask: Which of the following controls meet this requirement? (Select TWO)

options.why: A changed record no longer matches its stored hash, so the change is detected.
Fault tolerance keeps systems running through failures; it does not detect changes.
Redundant servers keep records reachable; they do not detect changes.
A signature fails to verify once the signed record changes.
Backup power keeps systems running, which serves availability.

detail: detect any change made to stored loan records
explain: Detecting change is integrity. Hashing and digital signatures both reveal when data has been altered.

ask: Which of the following does non-repudiation provide?

options.t: Proof that data was unchanged, with no proof of sender
options.why: That is what a hash alone gives: integrity without proof of who made it.

options.t: Proof of who sent data, which the sender cannot deny
options.why: Non-repudiation proves the origin and integrity of data so the sender cannot credibly deny it.

options.t: Assurance that data stays secret in transit
options.why: Keeping data secret is confidentiality, not proof of origin.

options.t: Assurance that a service stays reachable
options.why: Keeping a service reachable is availability, not proof of origin.

explain: Non-repudiation ties data to its sender with proof a third party can check, so the sender cannot later deny having sent or signed it.

ask: Which of the following explains why a shared symmetric key cannot provide non-repudiation?

options.t: Symmetric keys are too short to trust
options.why: Key length is not the issue; the problem is that the key is shared.

options.t: Symmetric keys cannot detect any changes
options.why: Shared-key methods such as HMAC do reveal changes; their weakness is that two parties hold the key.

options.t: Either key holder could have made the output
options.why: The key is shared, so the output could come from either party and points to no single sender.

options.t: Symmetric keys only protect stored data
options.why: Symmetric keys protect data in transit as well; the problem is that the key is shared.

explain: Non-repudiation needs a secret only the signer holds. A symmetric key is held by both parties, so either could have created the result.

stem: A sales director at a printing company insists he never sent a price quote that a customer received from his account. The company wants proof of the sender that an outside party can check.
ask: Which of the following would have given the company that proof?

options.t: A digital signature on the quote
options.why: Only the director's private key could create the signature, and anyone with his public key can verify it.
Anyone can compute a hash, so it shows the quote is unchanged but not who sent it.
Encryption keeps the quote secret; it does not prove who sent it.

options.t: A redundant copy of the quote
options.why: A second copy keeps the quote available; it proves nothing about the sender.

detail: proof of the sender that an outside party can check
explain: A digital signature made with the sender's private key gives non-repudiation: a third party can verify it, and the sender cannot credibly deny it.

stem: A release engineer at a game studio publishes a hash beside each download so players can check for tampering. A partner asks whether the hashes also prove the studio produced the files.
ask: Which of the following is accurate about the published hashes?

options.t: They prove integrity but not origin
options.why: Anyone can compute a hash, so it gives integrity but not proof of origin.

options.t: They prove both integrity and origin
options.why: A hash proves integrity only; proving origin needs a private key, as in a digital signature.

options.t: They keep the files secret from players
options.why: A hash does not hide the files; secrecy is confidentiality.

options.t: They keep the download site reachable
options.why: A hash does nothing for availability.

detail: whether the hashes also prove the studio produced the files
explain: A hash alone gives integrity but not non-repudiation. To prove the studio made the files, it would sign them with its private key.

stem: A loan officer at a bank approves wire transfers in a system that shares one secret key with every officer. If an approval is disputed later, an auditor must be able to confirm exactly which officer approved it.
ask: Which of the following should replace the shared key approach?

options.why: An HMAC uses a shared key, so the system or any key holder could have produced the tag.
A hash shows the approval is unchanged but says nothing about who approved it.
Each officer signs with a private key no one else holds, so the auditor can tie each approval to one officer.
A shared symmetric key cannot single out one officer, and encryption hides data rather than proving origin.

detail: confirm exactly which officer approved it
explain: Non-repudiation requires a key only one person holds. Digital signatures use each signer's private key; HMAC and symmetric methods share the key.

stem: A contracts manager at an engineering firm receives a supplier agreement signed with the supplier's private key. She checks the signature with the supplier's public key, and it verifies.
ask: Which of the following does the successful check show?

options.t: The agreement was kept secret in transit
options.why: A signature does not encrypt; secrecy in transit is confidentiality.

options.t: Its origin is proven and its text is unaltered
options.why: Only the supplier's private key could make a signature that verifies with its public key, and any change would break it.

options.t: Anyone holding the public key could have signed it
options.why: The public key only verifies; signing needs the private key, which only the supplier holds.

options.t: Only the contracts manager can read it
options.why: The signature does not restrict who can read the agreement.

detail: it verifies
explain: A valid signature proves the data came from the private key holder and was not changed, which is what non-repudiation rests on.

stem: A security officer at a notary service learns that a notary's private signing key was copied from an unprotected laptop last month.
ask: Which of the following is the main effect on documents signed with that key since then?

options.t: Their contents are now readable by anyone
options.why: A signature never hid the contents, so the copied key changes nothing about secrecy.

options.t: Their signatures will no longer verify
options.why: The signatures still verify with the public key; the problem is that someone else could have made them.

options.t: Their hashes no longer match the documents
options.why: Copying a key does not change the documents, so their hashes still match.

options.t: The signer can credibly deny making them
options.why: Once someone else holds the key, a valid signature no longer proves the notary made it.

detail: private signing key was copied
explain: Non-repudiation depends on the private key staying private. A stolen key lets the signer credibly deny signatures made after the theft.

stem: A paralegal at a law firm sends settlement offers by email. The receiving firm must be able to prove later that each offer came from her and was not altered.
ask: Which of the following should the paralegal do?

options.t: Encrypt each email with the recipient's public key
options.why: That keeps the email secret, but anyone could encrypt with a public key, so it proves nothing about the sender.

options.t: Attach a hash of each email
options.why: Anyone could compute and attach a hash, so it does not prove she sent it.

options.t: Sign each email with her private key
options.why: A signature from her private key proves she sent it and that it was not altered.

options.t: Protect each email with a shared HMAC key
options.why: Both firms hold the shared key, so the receiving firm could have made the tag itself.

detail: prove later that each offer came from her and was not altered
explain: Signing with her private key gives integrity and non-repudiation. Encryption, a plain hash or a shared key cannot single her out as the sender.

stem: A buyer at a hardware wholesaler opens an emailed price change and sees the status lines below.
ask: Which of the following does this email provide?

lines: Certificate issuer: Supplier Example Issuing CA

options.why: A valid signature tied to the sender's certificate proves who sent it, so the sender cannot credibly deny it.
The last line shows no encryption, so the email was not kept secret.
Nothing in the lines concerns keeping a service reachable.
Accounting logs what users did on a system; a signed email is not an access log.

detail: Signature: valid, signed by d.okafor@supplier.example
explain: A valid digital signature proves the sender and that the message is unchanged. With no encryption, the content was not kept confidential.

ask: Which of the following statements about non-repudiation are accurate? (Select TWO)

options.t: An HMAC tag can provide it
options.why: An HMAC uses a shared key, so either party could have made the tag.

options.t: It depends on the private key staying private
options.why: If the private key is stolen, the signer can credibly deny the signature.

options.t: A plain hash can provide it
options.why: Anyone can compute a hash, so it proves integrity only.
Encryption gives confidentiality; non-repudiation comes from signing.

options.t: A digital signature can provide it
options.why: A signature made with a private key proves who signed and that nothing changed.

explain: Non-repudiation comes from digital signatures, which rely on a private key only the signer holds. Hashes and HMACs prove integrity but not who acted.

ask: Which of the following AAA functions decides what a user who has proven an identity may do?

options.why: Authentication proves who the user is; it does not decide their rights.
Accounting records what the user did; it does not decide what is allowed.
Identification is only the claim of an identity, such as typing a username.
Authorization decides what an authenticated user is allowed to do.

explain: Authentication proves who someone is, authorization decides what they may do, and accounting records what they did.

ask: Which of the following gives the order of the AAA steps after a user claims an identity?

options.why: Rights cannot be decided for an identity that has not been proven yet.
The identity is proven first, then rights are decided, then activity is recorded.
Accounting records what was done, so it cannot come before access is granted.
Rights are decided before the session is recorded, so accounting comes last.

explain: After identification, the order is authentication, authorization and accounting. A system cannot decide rights for an identity it has not verified.

stem: A network administrator at a city transit agency needs a record of when each VPN session started and stopped and how much data it moved.
ask: Which of the following AAA functions provides this record?

options.why: Authorization decides what the user may reach; it does not record the session.
Accounting logs session start, stop and data use.
Authentication proves who connected; it does not track the session afterward.
Identification is the username claim; it records nothing.

detail: how much data it moved
explain: Accounting records what users did: logins, session times and resources used.

stem: A visiting researcher at a university logs in successfully with her username and password, but her request to open the grants database is refused.
ask: Which of the following AAA functions refused the request?

options.why: Authentication succeeded; the stem says she logged in successfully.
Accounting records activity; it does not grant or refuse requests.
Identification is only the username claim, which was already accepted.
She proved her identity, but authorization decided she may not open that database.

detail: logs in successfully
explain: Being authenticated does not mean being authorized. Authorization decides what a proven identity may do.

stem: A security analyst at a water utility pulls the stored session records each quarter and reads through them looking for misuse of administrator accounts.
ask: Which of the following BEST describes the analyst's quarterly work?

options.why: Reviewing collected records to find misuse is auditing.
Accounting produced the session records, but the stem asks about reading through them, which is a review.
Authorization decides what accounts may do; the analyst is not granting rights.
Authentication proves identities at login; the analyst is not logging anyone in.

detail: reads through them looking for misuse
edge: Accounting collects the records; reviewing them afterward for misuse is auditing.
explain: Accounting and auditing are separate steps: accounting creates the records, and auditing reviews them.

stem: A help desk technician at a dental group explains that the name a user types first proves nothing by itself, and the user must then show something that backs the claim.
ask: Which of the following steps does entering that name alone accomplish?

options.why: Authentication is the next step, when the user backs the claim with a factor.
Authorization decides rights after the identity is proven.
Typing a username is the claim of an identity, which is identification.
Accounting records activity during the session.

detail: proves nothing by itself
explain: Identification is the claim; authentication proves it. A username is public, so it cannot prove anything alone.

stem: A systems administrator at a call center wants one central server to check VPN logins, place each user in an access group, and log each session for every remote office.
ask: Which of the following would provide all three functions?

options.why: A certificate authority issues certificates; it does not assign groups or log sessions.
A syslog server stores logs, but it does not check logins or assign access.
A web proxy relays web traffic; it does not authenticate VPN users or assign access groups.
A RADIUS server handles authentication, authorization and accounting for network access.

detail: log each session for every remote office
explain: RADIUS is a common AAA server: it checks credentials, returns the user's access, and records accounting data for each session.

stem: A network manager at a telecom configures TACACS+ so that every command an engineer types on a core switch is checked against the engineer's permitted command list before it runs.
ask: Which of the following AAA functions performs the per-command check?

options.why: Authentication happened once at login; it does not judge each command.
Deciding whether each command is allowed is authorization.
Accounting records the commands after they run; it does not allow or refuse them.
Identification is the username claim at the start of the session.

detail: checked against the engineer's permitted command list before it runs
explain: TACACS+ separates the three AAA functions, so each command can be authorized on its own and also recorded by accounting.

stem: A network administrator at a freight railroad reads the AAA server records below.
ask: Which of the following AAA functions decided the outcome on the first line?

options.why: Authorization decided lines 2 and 3, where commands were permitted or denied.
Accounting wrote these records, but it did not decide to accept the login.
Accepting the login means the user's proof of identity was verified, which is authentication.
Identification is only the username claim; accepting the login required proof.

detail: login=accepted
explain: Line 1 is the authentication result, lines 2 and 3 are authorization decisions, and the records themselves are accounting.

ask: Which of the following are examples of accounting? (Select TWO)

options.t: Checking a password against a stored hash
options.why: Verifying a password proves identity, which is authentication.

options.t: Placing a user in a group allowed to reach a share
options.why: Granting access through a group is authorization.

options.t: Logging session start and stop times
options.why: Recording when sessions began and ended is accounting.

options.t: Recording how much data a user moved
options.why: Tracking resources used is accounting.

options.t: Typing a username at the login screen
options.why: Claiming an identity is identification.

explain: Accounting records what users did, such as session times and data used. Proving identity is authentication and granting access is authorization.

ask: Which of the following combinations is multifactor authentication?

options.t: Password plus a phone app code
options.why: A password is something you know and the phone is something you have: two different factor types.
Both are something you know, so this is still one factor type.
Two passwords are the same factor type, which is not MFA.
The username only identifies; the password is the single factor.

explain: Multifactor authentication (MFA) combines different factor types, such as something you know with something you have.

ask: Which of the following factor types is a fingerprint scan?

options.why: A fingerprint is a biometric trait of the person.
Knowledge factors are things remembered, such as a password.
Possession factors are objects held, such as a phone or token.
This refers to location, not a body trait.

explain: Biometrics such as fingerprints are something you are; passwords are something you know; tokens and phones are something you have.

stem: An office manager at a veterinary clinic signs in to the records system by typing a password and then pressing a finger on a reader.
ask: Which of the following describes this sign-in?

options.why: Two different factor types are used, so it is more than one factor.
Authorization decides what she may do after sign-in; the stem describes proving who she is.
A password (something you know) plus a fingerprint (something you are) are two different factor types.
Accounting records activity; the stem describes proving identity.

detail: typing a password and then pressing a finger on a reader
explain: Combining a knowledge factor with a biometric is multifactor authentication.

stem: An IT coordinator at a school district notices that the staff portal asks for a password and then for the name of the first school each person attended.
ask: Which of the following describes the portal's sign-in?

options.why: Two items of the same factor type are not MFA.
Both the password and the school name are something you know, so only one factor type is used.
Authorization decides rights after sign-in; the portal is proving identity.
Identification is only the username claim; the portal is asking for proof.

detail: the name of the first school each person attended
explain: A password plus a personal question is two knowledge items. MFA needs different factor types.

stem: A security engineer at a payment processor must add a second factor to administrator logins that already use a password.
ask: Which of the following would satisfy the requirement?

options.why: A longer password is still the same factor.
A question is something you know, the same type as the password.
A passphrase is something you know, the same type as the password.
A token is something you have, a different type from the password.

detail: add a second factor
explain: A second factor must be a different type. With a password (know) in place, a token (have) or a biometric (are) adds a real second factor.

stem: An identity administrator at an architecture firm points out that staff usernames appear in every email signature the firm sends.
ask: Which of the following explains why a username alone cannot authenticate a user?

options.why: A username is not an object the user holds.
A username is not a body trait.

options.t: It is only a claim of identity
options.why: A username identifies the user; it is public, so it proves nothing.
Deciding rights is authorization; a username does neither.

detail: usernames appear in every email signature
explain: Identification is the claim, such as a username. Authentication requires proof, such as a password, token or biometric.

stem: A plant manager at a chemical maker wants floor supervisors to sign in at control stations with a smart card and a fingerprint.
ask: Which of the following factor types does this combine?

options.t: Something you have and something you are
options.why: A smart card is held (have) and a fingerprint is a trait (are).

options.t: Something you know and something you are
options.why: No password or other remembered item is used.

options.t: Something you have and something you know
options.why: A fingerprint is a trait, not something remembered.

options.t: Two instances of something you have
options.why: A fingerprint is not an object held.

detail: a smart card and a fingerprint
explain: Smart cards are possession factors and fingerprints are inherence (biometric) factors, so this is MFA across two types.

stem: A phishing email gave an outsider the password of a sales representative at a car dealership. The sales system also requires a code from an app on the representative's registered phone.
ask: Which of the following stops the outsider from signing in?

options.t: The length of the stolen password
options.why: The outsider already holds the password, so its length no longer helps.
Encryption hides traffic in transit; it does not stop someone holding a valid password.
Accounting records the attempt; it does not block it.
Without the registered phone, the outsider cannot supply the second factor.

detail: requires a code from an app on the representative's registered phone
explain: A phished password is one factor. MFA means the attacker also needs something of a different type, here the phone.

stem: A security consultant at a regional insurer reviews the remote access settings below.
ask: Which of the following describes the sign-in these settings enforce?

options.why: Step 2 is the same factor type as step 1, so this is not MFA.
Both steps are something you know, so only one factor type is checked.
Step 1 is a password, so the sign-in is not passwordless.
Nothing changes with context or risk; every sign-in gets the same two steps.

detail: step2 = personal question (city of birth)
explain: A password plus a personal question is two knowledge items, which is single-factor. The lockout limits guessing but adds no factor.

ask: Which of the following pairs count as multifactor authentication? (Select TWO)

options.why: A card (have) and a passcode (know) are two different types.
Both are something you know.
A fingerprint (are) and a token (have) are two different types.
Both are something you know.
Both are something you have.

explain: MFA requires factors of different types. Two items of the same type, however many, remain one factor type.

ask: Which of the following is commonly used to authenticate a device on a corporate network?

options.t: A host name in a network list
options.why: A host name is just a label any device can claim; it proves nothing.

options.t: A certificate from the company CA
options.why: A device certificate signed by the organization's CA proves the device is a trusted one.
A password authenticates the person, not the device.

options.t: A serial number on the device label
options.why: A printed serial number can be read and copied; it is not proof.

explain: Devices cannot type passwords, so they are usually authenticated with digital certificates issued by the organization's certificate authority.

ask: Which of the following questions does authenticating systems answer?

options.t: Is this user who they claim?
options.why: That is authenticating people.
That is authorization.
That is accounting.

options.t: Is this device one of ours?
options.why: Authenticating systems verifies that a device is the trusted one it claims to be.

explain: Authenticating systems answers how the organization knows a device is its own; user authentication, authorization and accounting answer other questions.

stem: A network engineer at a marine shipping firm sets the VPN concentrator to admit only laptops that present a certificate signed by the internal CA.
ask: Which of the following does this setting perform?

options.why: Checking that each laptop holds a certificate from the internal CA verifies the device itself.
The certificate belongs to the laptop, not to the person using it.
The check proves which device is connecting; it does not decide what a user may open.
Accounting records sessions; the setting checks the device's identity.

detail: admit only laptops that present a certificate signed by the internal CA
explain: Device certificates signed by a trusted CA are the common way to authenticate systems, for example at a VPN.

stem: A security administrator at a cooperative bank must stop staff from reaching back-office apps from personal laptops, even when they enter a valid password and approve a phone prompt.
ask: Which of the following meets this requirement?

options.why: A stronger password still works from a personal laptop.
Another user factor proves the person, not which laptop is used.
Only company laptops hold a certificate from the organization's CA, so personal laptops fail the check.
Logs record activity but do not block a personal laptop.

detail: even when they enter a valid password and approve a phone prompt
explain: User factors prove the person. To know the device is the company's own, the device must authenticate, usually with a certificate.

stem: A wireless administrator at a university must admit only university-owned tablets to the staff network. The network must also reject any tablet that copies an owned tablet's hardware address.
ask: Which of the following BEST meets these requirements?

options.why: It admits listed tablets, but a MAC address can be copied, which the stem says must be rejected.
Anyone given the passphrase can join from any device.
A captive portal collects a login or agreement; it does not prove the device is owned.
A copied hardware address does not give a device the certificate's private key, so only owned tablets pass.

detail: reject any tablet that copies an owned tablet's hardware address
edge: MAC filtering limits the network to known addresses, but addresses can be spoofed. A certificate needs a private key that copying an address does not give.
explain: A MAC address is an identifier, not proof. Device certificates signed by the organization's CA prove ownership.

stem: A PKI engineer at an aerospace supplier is asked why each device must sign a challenge when it connects, instead of only sending its certificate.
ask: Which of the following explains the challenge step?

options.t: It encrypts the certificate for transit
options.why: Certificates are public; the step is about proof, not secrecy.

options.t: It proves possession of the private key
options.why: A certificate can be copied; signing a challenge shows the device has the matching private key.

options.t: It renews the certificate before expiry
options.why: Renewal is a separate process; the challenge happens at every connection.

options.t: It hides the device's host name
options.why: The challenge does not hide any name; it proves key possession.

detail: instead of only sending its certificate
explain: A certificate alone proves nothing, since it is public. The device must show it holds the private key that matches it.

stem: A network team at a hospital requires both a device certificate and the nurse's MFA before anyone reaches the charting app.
ask: Which of the following does the device certificate add that the nurse's MFA does not?

options.t: Proof of who the user is
options.why: The nurse's MFA already proves the person.

options.t: A record of what was opened
options.why: Recording activity is accounting, not part of device authentication.
The certificate shows the hardware is a managed device.
Keeping stored records secret is confidentiality through encryption, not a device check.

detail: both a device certificate and the nurse's MFA
explain: Device authentication and user authentication answer different questions, so many networks require both.

stem: A web developer at an online pharmacy wants customers' browsers to confirm they reached the real checkout server and not an impostor.
ask: Which of the following provides this assurance?

options.t: A certificate from a trusted CA
options.why: The browser checks that the server's certificate chains to a trusted CA, proving the server's identity.
A password proves the customer, not the server.

options.t: A hash shown on the checkout page

An address is an identifier, not proof; it can be spoofed or redirected.

stem: A systems engineer at a grocery chain inspects a point-of-sale terminal and finds the details below.
ask: Which of the following is this item used for?

lines: Private key: non-exportable, stored in TPM

options.why: A client certificate from the retailer's device CA lets the network verify the device.

explain: A device certificate issued by the organization's CA, with its private key kept in hardware, authenticates the device to the network.

ask: Which of the following are accurate about device certificates? (Select TWO)

options.t: A copied certificate alone is enough to connect
options.why: Without the private key, a copied certificate fails the challenge.

options.t: They are signed by a CA the network trusts
options.why: The network accepts devices whose certificate chains to the trusted CA.

options.t: They remove the need for user authentication
options.why: Device and user authentication answer different questions; many networks require both.

options.t: The device must prove it holds the private key
options.why: A copied certificate without its private key proves nothing.

options.t: A MAC address serves the same purpose
options.why: A MAC address is an identifier that can be copied, not proof.

explain: Device certificates come from a CA the network trusts, and the device proves it holds the private key. They complement user authentication.

ask: Which of the following describes an authorization model?

options.t: Rights granted to each user for each resource
options.why: Granting rights one by one is the direct approach that models replace because it does not scale.

options.t: Proof of identity with one or more factors
options.why: Proving identity is authentication, which happens before any model runs.

options.t: Rights mapped to users through roles or groups
options.why: A model places an abstraction such as a role or group between users and permissions.

options.t: A record of what each user did and when
options.why: Recording activity is accounting.

explain: Authorization models map users to permissions through roles, groups, attributes or rules instead of per-user grants.

ask: What is the main benefit of granting rights to roles instead of to individual users?

options.t: It removes the need to authenticate
options.why: Users must still prove who they are before any rights apply.

options.t: It scales and is easier to audit
options.why: One role grant covers many users, and reviewers can see who has what by role.
Roles organize permissions; they do not encrypt anything.

options.t: It logs every action users take
options.why: Logging actions is accounting, a separate function.

explain: Abstraction through roles or groups scales to many users and resources and is easier to audit than per-user grants.

stem: A systems administrator at a food distributor must give every new warehouse picker the same access to the inventory app and two shared folders.
ask: Which of the following approaches follows an authorization model?

options.t: Grant each picker rights to each resource
options.why: Per-user grants are the approach models replace; they do not scale.

options.t: Give all pickers one shared account
options.why: A shared account hides who did what and is not a model of mapping users to rights.

options.t: Copy rights from a coworker for each picker
options.why: Copying rights person by person is still per-user granting.

options.t: Grant rights to a picker role and add staff to it
options.why: Rights go to the role once, and each new picker gets them by joining the role.

detail: every new warehouse picker the same access
explain: Granting rights to a role and adding users to it is the abstraction an authorization model provides.

stem: When a payroll specialist at an airline moves to the marketing team, an administrator removes her from one group, and every payroll right she had disappears at once.
ask: Which of the following explains why one change removed all of those rights?

options.t: Her rights were tied to her password
options.why: A password proves identity; it does not carry any rights.
Accounting records what she did; clearing them removes no rights.

options.t: Her rights came through the group
options.why: Her payroll rights were granted to the group, so leaving it removed them all.

options.t: Each of her rights was revoked separately
options.why: The stem says one change removed all of them, not many separate revocations.

detail: removes her from one group
explain: When rights belong to a group or role, membership is the single switch that grants or removes them all.

stem: An identity engineer at a bus manufacturer assigns permissions to job functions such as welding supervisor and quality inspector, and each employee receives the permissions of the job held.
ask: Which of the following access control models is in use?

options.why: Permissions attached to job functions that staff receive by job is role-based access control.
In discretionary access control, resource owners grant access themselves, not by job function.
Mandatory access control uses labels and clearances, not job functions.
Rule-based access control applies system rules such as times or addresses, not job functions.

detail: assigns permissions to job functions
explain: Role-based access control (RBAC) grants permissions to roles that match job functions, and users inherit them through their role.

stem: A security analyst at a semiconductor fab finds that 1,200 users each hold rights granted one by one across 300 shares, and no one can say who has access to what.
ask: Which of the following changes addresses this problem?

options.why: MFA strengthens login but leaves the tangle of per-user rights in place.
Logs show what users did, not what they are allowed to do.

options.t: Encrypt the contents of every share
options.why: Encryption protects confidentiality; it does not organize who has access.
Moving rights onto roles makes access readable by role and easier to audit.

detail: no one can say who has access to what
explain: Per-user grants do not scale and cannot be audited. An authorization model groups rights so access can be read and reviewed.

stem: A developer at an insurance startup proposes checking a caller's role before verifying the caller's login token, to save time on each request.
ask: Which of the following is the problem with this design?

options.t: Roles cannot be stored alongside login tokens
options.why: Where roles are stored is not the issue; the order of the checks is.

options.t: Rights cannot be decided for an unproven identity
options.why: Authorization must follow authentication; until the token is verified, the role claim may be false.

options.t: Accounting must run before any check
options.why: Accounting records the session after access is decided, not first.

options.t: Login tokens are a knowledge factor
options.why: Whether a token counts as a factor is not the issue; the problem is checking the role before the token is verified.

detail: checking a caller's role before verifying the caller's login token
explain: An authorization model runs only after identity is proven. Checking the role first trusts a claim nobody has verified.

stem: An operations manager at a bakery chain asks whether a cashier who has already signed in successfully may also void sales at the register.
ask: Which of the following AAA functions answers this question?

options.why: The cashier has already signed in, so identity is settled.
Deciding what a signed-in user may do, such as void sales, is authorization.
Accounting would record a void after it happens; it does not decide whether it is allowed.
Identification is the claim of an identity, which happened at sign-in.

detail: may also void sales
explain: Authentication proves who the cashier is; the authorization model then decides which actions, such as voids, are allowed.

explain: Rights granted to a role reach users only through membership, so one removal ends all of them for that user.

ask: Which of the following are benefits of assigning permissions through roles? (Select TWO)

options.t: Removes the need to authenticate users
options.why: Users must still prove their identity before rights apply.
Recording activity is accounting.

options.t: Easier to audit who has what
options.why: Reviewers can read access by role instead of by thousands of separate grants.
Roles exist to give each group only what its job needs.

options.t: Scales to many users and resources
options.why: One grant to a role covers every member.

explain: Role-based grants scale and are easier to audit than per-user permissions. They do not replace authentication or accounting.

ask: Which of the following describes a security gap analysis?

options.t: Comparing current controls with a target standard
options.why: A gap analysis compares the current posture with a desired state to find what is missing.

options.t: Testing whether attacks against systems succeed
options.why: Trying attacks is penetration testing, which does not measure against a standard.

options.t: Scanning hosts for known software flaws
options.why: Finding technical flaws on hosts is a vulnerability scan, not a program-wide comparison.

options.t: Recording who signed in and when
options.why: Recording sign-ins is accounting.

explain: A gap analysis measures the distance between where security is now and a target, such as a framework, and plans how to close it.

ask: What does a gap analysis usually produce?

options.why: Formal certification comes from an audit; a gap analysis prepares for one.

options.t: A list of hosts that were broken into
options.why: That would come from a penetration test.

options.t: A prioritized plan to close the gaps
options.why: The result is a roadmap that ranks the gaps and plans how to close them.

options.t: A log of each user's sessions
options.why: Session logs are accounting records.

explain: A gap analysis ends in a plan or roadmap, usually with the worst gaps first.

stem: A compliance manager at a robotics maker lists each requirement in an industry standard, notes which ones the company already meets, and marks the rest for a project plan.
ask: Which of the following describes the manager's work?

options.why: Nothing is being attacked; requirements are being compared.
No hosts are being scanned; the manager is comparing practices with a standard.

options.t: Reviewing logs for signs of misuse
options.why: Log review looks at past activity, not at how the program compares with a standard.

options.t: Measuring the distance from a target baseline
options.why: Comparing what is met against the standard's requirements, then planning the rest, is a gap analysis.

detail: notes which ones the company already meets
explain: A gap analysis compares the current state with a target baseline and turns the differences into a plan.

options.t: So attackers cannot read the report
options.why: Colors do not protect the report; they rank the findings.

options.t: So each area gets the same budget
options.why: The point of ranking is to spend first where the gaps are biggest, not equally.

detail: colors each area of the result green, yellow or red
explain: Gap analysis results are often scored per area so the organization fixes the most serious gaps first.

stem: The security director at a card payment processor wants to know how far the whole security program is from the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, covering policies, staff training and technology.
ask: Which of the following BEST meets this need?

options.why: A scan finds technical flaws on hosts, but it says nothing about policies or training.
Trying attacks examines part of the technology, but it does not measure policies or training against a framework.
Comparing the whole program against a framework, people and process included, is a gap analysis.
A tabletop exercise rehearses incident response; it does not compare the program with a framework.

edge: A vulnerability scan covers part of the technology, but the stem asks about the whole program, including policies and training.
explain: A gap analysis measures the distance between the current program and a target framework across people, process and technology.

stem: A newly hired security manager at a cruise line is asked to run the company's first gap analysis.
ask: Which of the following should the manager do FIRST?

options.t: Choose the framework to measure against

options.t: Buy tools for the largest gaps
options.why: The gaps are not known yet; buying first skips the comparison.

options.t: Rate each gap red, yellow or green
options.why: Gaps can be rated only after the comparison finds them.

options.t: Write the action plan with owners
options.why: The action plan comes last, after the gaps are found and ranked.

detail: first gap analysis
explain: A gap analysis starts by setting the scope and the target baseline, then gathers evidence, compares, rates the gaps and writes the plan.

stem: Months before an independent external audit, a compliance lead at a medical laboratory compares current practices with the standard so the weaknesses can be fixed in time.
ask: Which of the following is the compliance lead carrying out?

options.why: An internal comparison against the standard to find and fix weaknesses ahead of an audit is a gap analysis.
The external audit is the later, independent check; the lead is preparing for it.
No attacks are being tried; practices are being compared with a standard.
No hosts are being scanned for flaws.

explain: A gap analysis is often done before an audit to find and fix weaknesses. The audit is the formal, usually independent, check that follows.

stem: A risk analyst at a hotel group rates each likely threat to the reservation system by how likely it is and how much harm it would cause.

A scan finds flaws on hosts; it does not rate threats by likelihood.
Rating threats by likelihood and impact is a risk assessment.
A penetration test tries attacks; it does not score threats.

The phishing drill is the only area rated Red, the biggest gap.

ask: Which of the following are accurate about a gap analysis? (Select TWO)

options.t: It proves that attacks would fail
options.why: It compares controls with a target; it does not test attacks.
It often prepares for an audit, but it is not the formal check.

options.t: It is a scan of hosts for flaws
options.why: That is a vulnerability scan.

options.t: It can take weeks or months
options.why: A full analysis of a program takes time.

ask: Which of the following describes the Zero Trust security model?

options.t: Users inside the network are trusted
options.why: Trusting the inside is the old perimeter model that Zero Trust replaces.

options.t: No request is trusted by default, even inside
options.why: Zero Trust authenticates, authorizes and checks every request, wherever it comes from.

options.t: Trust is granted once a day at first login
options.why: Zero Trust checks each request; it does not hand out a day of trust.

options.t: Only traffic from the internet is checked
options.why: Zero Trust checks internal requests as well; location grants no trust.

explain: Zero Trust means never trust, always verify: every subject and request is checked, with no implicit trust from network location.

ask: Which of the following describes how a Zero Trust architecture is split?

options.t: Data plane decides, control plane enforces
options.why: This reverses the roles: deciding is the control plane's job.

options.t: Inside zone decides, outside zone enforces
options.why: Zero Trust does not split trust by inside and outside.

options.t: Control plane decides and also enforces
options.why: Enforcement happens in the data plane, where the traffic flows.

options.t: Control plane decides, data plane enforces
options.why: The control plane makes decisions; the data plane carries traffic and enforces them.

explain: Zero Trust separates a control plane that decides from a data plane that carries traffic and enforces the decision.

stem: A claims adjuster at an insurer works at the head office on the corporate network. Each time she opens the claims app, she must still sign in and pass a device health check.
ask: Which of the following explains why she is checked even on the corporate network?

options.why: Nothing in the stem says the account is suspect; the checks happen every time.

options.t: The claims app sits outside the office
options.why: Where the app is hosted does not change the rule; every request is checked.
Under Zero Trust, being inside the network does not earn trust, so every request is checked.

options.t: Head office devices are trusted by default
options.why: If they were trusted by default, she would not be checked.

stem: A pharmacist at a hospital opens the dispensing app from a ward workstation, and the request is checked against her identity and the workstation's state before access is granted, every time.
ask: Which of the following principles does this reflect?

options.why: Every request is verified, with no trust carried over from earlier requests or from location.
The stem says the check happens every time, not once.
The workstation is inside the building and is still checked.
She is on a ward workstation, not remote, and is still verified.

detail: every time
explain: Never trust, always verify is the core of Zero Trust: identity and device are checked per request.

stem: A network manager at a game studio already requires the corporate VPN for remote staff. The manager now wants each request to each app checked for identity and device posture, wherever the user is.
ask: Which of the following describes the model the manager wants?

A screened subnet is a network zone for public-facing servers, not a per-request check.
A VPN joins networks; it does not check each request to each app.
Checking every request for identity and device posture, regardless of location, is Zero Trust.

detail: wherever the user is
explain: Zero Trust moves the checks to each request and each resource, so being on the VPN or the office network grants nothing by itself.

stem: At a trade show, a vendor tells an IT director at a credit union that buying one appliance will make the network Zero Trust.

options.t: Zero Trust is a model, not one product
options.why: Zero Trust is a set of principles and an architecture; no single box delivers it.

options.t: Zero Trust removes the need for firewalls
options.why: Firewalls and segmentation stay; they stop being the only gate.

options.t: Zero Trust means never trusting any user
options.why: Trust is earned per request, not refused forever.

detail: buying one appliance will make the network Zero Trust
explain: Zero Trust is a model and set of principles. Products can help, but it is not something bought in one box.

stem: After an attacker stole a contractor's VPN password at an electric utility, the security team found the attacker could reach every internal system once connected.

options.why: A gap analysis plans improvements; it does not check each request.

stem: A cloud architect at a biotech firm explains to new staff that the firm's Zero Trust design still uses firewalls and network segmentation.

options.t: They remain, but are not the only gate
