stem: A risk analyst at a regional credit union reviews five purchases proposed for its branches.
ask: Which of the following purchases are physical security controls? (Select TWO)

options.why: Encryption protects data with software, not a building or people.

options.t: A two-door entry booth for the vault
options.why: A two-door booth is a physical entry control that lets one person through at a time.
Multifactor sign-in authenticates users to a system; it is a technical control.
A written policy guides behavior; it is managerial, not a physical barrier or device.

options.t: Steel posts at the branch entrance
options.why: Posts are a physical barrier that keeps vehicles away from the building.

detail: five purchases proposed for its branches
explain: Posts and a two-door entry booth (bollards and an access control vestibule) protect the site physically. Encryption and sign-in are technical, a policy is managerial.

source.chapter: Physical access controls compared (bollards vs fencing vs access control vestibule vs guards vs badges)

ask: Which of the following describes bollards?

options.t: A two-door booth that admits one person at a time
options.why: That is an access control vestibule, which controls people at a door, not vehicles.

options.t: A tall barrier that keeps people off a whole site
options.why: That describes a fence along a perimeter; bollards let people walk between them.

options.t: Short, sturdy posts that stop cars but let walkers pass
options.why: Bollards are short, strong posts spaced so a vehicle cannot pass but a person on foot can.

options.t: A floor mat that reports weight placed on it
options.why: That is a pressure sensor, which detects a person rather than stopping a vehicle.

explain: Bollards are short, sturdy posts placed to stop vehicles from reaching a building or area while people on foot still pass between them.

ask: What is a row of bollards designed to stop?

options.why: Bollards leave gaps so people on foot can pass; they are not meant to stop them.
Bollards are spaced and anchored to stop cars and trucks.
Someone following another person through a door is stopped by an access control vestibule.
People climbing over a boundary are slowed by a tall fence, not by short posts.

explain: Bollards stop vehicles, not people. They protect entrances, glass fronts and equipment from cars driven into them.

stem: The manager of a garden center wants to keep cars in the parking lot from being driven into the glass front of the greenhouse. Shoppers must still be able to walk in freely.
ask: Which of the following should the manager install?

options.t: A row of short steel posts
options.why: Short steel posts block a car but leave gaps that shoppers walk through.
An entry booth controls one person at a time at a door; it does nothing about cars.
A tall barrier would also keep shoppers out, which the manager does not want.

options.t: A badge reader on the door
options.why: A badge reader controls who opens a door; it cannot stop a car hitting the glass.

detail: Shoppers must still be able to walk in freely
explain: Bollards stop vehicles while letting people on foot pass, which matches both needs: no cars into the glass, free walking access.

stem: A planner at a transit authority places short steel posts outside a busy station so that no car can drive into the crowd. The posts are spaced so that riders move in an orderly line toward the ticket gates.
ask: Which other purpose do the posts serve in this design?

options.t: Guiding the movement of people on foot
options.why: Bollards can also channel foot traffic, here into a line toward the gates.

options.t: Holding each rider for an identity check
options.why: Holding a person for a check is what a two-door vestibule does, not a row of posts.

options.t: Recording which riders enter the station
options.why: Posts record nothing; a camera or badge system would keep a record.

options.t: Detecting riders who carry metal objects
options.why: Posts sense nothing; they are passive physical barriers.

detail: riders move in an orderly line toward the ticket gates
explain: Besides stopping vehicles, bollards are used to channel foot traffic along a chosen path.

stem: After steel posts are installed in front of a pharmacy, an auditor notes that they do nothing to stop a person who walks up to the door. The store manager asks whether the posts were a mistake.
ask: Which of the following explains why the posts still serve their purpose?

options.t: They are meant to record who walks past
options.why: Posts record nothing, so this cannot be their purpose.

options.t: They are meant to stop vehicles, not people
options.why: Bollards are built to stop cars; letting people walk past them is by design.

options.t: They are meant to hold each visitor for a check
options.why: Posts hold no one; a two-door vestibule does that at a door.

options.t: They are meant to alert staff when touched
options.why: Plain posts raise no alert; they are a passive barrier.

detail: they do nothing to stop a person who walks up to the door
explain: Bollards stop vehicles, not people. A person walking to the door is expected to pass, so the auditor's note is no sign of a mistake.

stem: The facilities manager of a city library must keep vehicles off the paved plaza in front of the building. A delivery van still has to reach the loading door across the plaza each morning.
ask: Which of the following meets both needs?

options.t: Fixed bollards across the whole plaza
options.why: Fixed posts everywhere would also block the delivery van every morning.

options.t: A fence around the whole plaza
options.why: A fence would keep library visitors off the plaza as well.

options.t: Fixed bollards with one that can be lowered
options.why: Fixed posts keep vehicles out, and the one that lowers lets the van through when staff allow it.

options.t: A camera watching the whole plaza
options.why: A camera records vehicles on the plaza but does not stop them.

detail: A delivery van still has to reach the loading door
explain: Fixed bollards are permanent; retractable or removable ones can be lowered to let an authorized vehicle through.

stem: A facilities engineer at a data center must protect the outdoor generators and fuel tank that sit beside the service road. The concern is a delivery truck that misjudges a turn and strikes them.
ask: Which of the following controls should the engineer install?

options.why: A fence controls people along a perimeter; it is not built to stop a truck.
Cameras would record the crash but not prevent it.
A pressure sensor reports weight at a spot; it cannot stop a truck.
Anchored posts stop a vehicle before it reaches the equipment.

detail: a delivery truck that misjudges a turn and strikes them
explain: Bollards keep vehicles from hitting critical equipment such as generators and fuel tanks, whether the impact is deliberate or an accident.

stem: A project manager at a convention center receives the contractor's work order below.
ask: Which threat does this work order address?

lines: Item 1  Set 18 steel posts along the main walkway to the doors
Item 2  Anchor each post in concrete, rated for impact
Item 3  Keep 1.5 m between posts for strollers and wheelchairs

options.why: Following someone through a door is stopped by a vestibule, not by posts outside.
Climbing a boundary is slowed by a tall fence; posts with gaps let people through.
Impact-rated posts with walking gaps are bollards, which stop vehicles.
Darkness is fixed with lighting; steel posts do not light anything.

detail: Anchor each post in concrete, rated for impact
explain: Anchored, impact-rated posts spaced for people on foot are bollards: they stop vehicles from reaching the entrance.

stem: A risk manager at a fuel station chain has concrete posts set in front of the shop windows at every station, so that no car can reach the glass.
ask: Which control type BEST describes the posts?

options.why: The posts physically stop a car before it reaches the glass, which is preventive.
Solid posts may discourage a driver, but the stated goal is that no car can reach the glass.
Posts detect nothing and raise no alert.
Posts act before any harm; they restore nothing afterward.

detail: so that no car can reach the glass
edge: Any visible barrier discourages a little, but the posts are there to physically stop the car, and stopping harm before it happens is preventive.
explain: Bollards are a preventive physical control: they block a vehicle before it can do harm.

stem: A parks department planner proposes a row of steel bollards between a playground and the busy road beside it.
ask: Which of the following statements about the planned bollards are accurate? (Select TWO)

options.t: They hold each person for an identity check
options.why: That is a vestibule at a door, not posts along a road.

options.t: They alert staff when someone climbs over
options.why: Bollards raise no alert, and they are not meant to be climbed over.

options.t: They keep cars from reaching the playground
options.why: Stopping vehicles is what bollards are built for.

options.t: They let children and parents walk between them
options.why: Bollards are spaced so people on foot can pass.

options.t: They record who enters the playground
options.why: Posts keep no record; a camera would.

detail: between a playground and the busy road
explain: Bollards stop vehicles while letting people on foot move freely, which protects the playground from the road without closing it off.

ask: Which of the following describes an access control vestibule?

options.t: A row of posts that keeps vehicles back
options.why: That describes bollards, which stop cars, not people at a door.

options.t: A lobby desk where visitors sign a book
options.why: A sign-in desk records visitors but holds no one between two doors.

options.t: A single door that opens for a valid badge
options.why: A single badge door lets a second person walk in behind the first, which a vestibule prevents.

options.t: A small space whose two doors open one at a time
options.why: A vestibule has two interlocking doors, and only one can be open at a time.

explain: An access control vestibule is a small space with two doors where only one can be open at a time, so each person is checked on their own.

ask: Which of the following is an access control vestibule mainly built to prevent?

options.t: A car being driven into a lobby
options.why: Keeping cars out of a lobby is the job of bollards.
Interlocking doors stop tailgating and piggybacking: each person passes and is checked alone.

options.t: A person climbing over a boundary
options.why: Climbing over a boundary is slowed by a tall fence, not by a doorway.

options.t: A visitor reading a screen from behind
options.why: Reading over someone's shoulder happens inside, after entry; door design does not address it.

explain: The vestibule exists to stop tailgating and piggybacking, where a second person gets in on someone else's entry.

stem: The facilities director of a genetics lab learns that staff often hold the secure door open for coworkers behind them. She wants each person checked on their own before entering.
ask: Which of the following should the director install?

options.why: Posts stop vehicles; staff on foot would still pass with the door held open.
Interlocking doors let only one checked person through at a time, so no one can be let in behind another.

options.t: A reminder sign on the door
options.why: A sign asks staff to stop but cannot enforce it; the door can still be held open.
A camera records people coming in behind others but does not stop them.

detail: She wants each person checked on their own before entering
explain: An access control vestibule enforces one entry per check with its interlocking doors, without relying on staff to refuse.

stem: At the records center of a mortgage lender, a records clerk badges through an outer door. She waits for it to close and lock, then badges again to open the inner door.
ask: Which of the following is the purpose of this two-step entry?

options.t: Stopping a vehicle from reaching the door
options.why: Doors that open in turn do nothing against vehicles; bollards do.

options.t: Recording the clerk's face on video
options.why: Nothing in the entry records video; the two doors control passage.

options.t: Marking the edge of the property
options.why: The entry sits at a building door, not along the property line.

options.t: Stopping anyone from following the clerk in
options.why: The inner door opens only after the outer one locks, so no one can slip in with her.

detail: waits for it to close and lock, then badges again to open the inner door
explain: This is an access control vestibule: interlocked doors and a second check let exactly one authorized person through.

stem: A security trainer at a freight company describes two incidents. In one, a stranger slipped in behind an employee without being noticed. In the other, an employee knowingly held the door for a friend.
ask: Which of the following would have stopped both incidents?

options.t: Two interlocking doors with a check
options.why: A vestibule stops both: it lets one checked person through, whether the follower is noticed or welcomed.

options.t: A reminder sign about holding doors
options.why: A sign does not stop a stranger who is not noticed, nor an employee who ignores it.
A camera records both incidents but stops neither.
Posts stop vehicles; both incidents were people on foot.

detail: an employee knowingly held the door for a friend
explain: Tailgating (unnoticed) and piggybacking (with consent) are both stopped by an access control vestibule, because the doors admit one checked person at a time.

stem: A compliance officer at a payment processor must meet a rule for the card vault room: one authorized person per check, and no one let in behind another. The rule must be enforced by the entrance itself, not by staff deciding to refuse.
ask: Which of the following controls BEST meets this rule?

options.why: A guard can turn away a follower, but that relies on a person deciding to refuse.
Cameras record a person who follows another in, but stop no one.
Its interlocking doors physically admit one checked person at a time, with no one needing to refuse.
A badge opens the door for its holder, and a second person can still walk in behind.

detail: enforced by the entrance itself, not by staff deciding to refuse
edge: A guard can stop a follower, but the rule asks for enforcement by the entrance itself, which only the interlocking doors provide.
explain: An access control vestibule enforces one entry per check physically, so it does not depend on people saying no.

stem: At the cash room of a casino, a person steps into a small room through one door. A guard behind glass checks the person's ID, and only then releases the second door.
ask: Which of the following describes the small room with two doors?

options.why: Bollards are posts that stop vehicles, not rooms that hold people.
Fencing runs along a perimeter; it is not a room at a door.
Nothing here records video; the guard checks an ID before releasing the door.
A small room between two doors, with a check before the second opens, is a vestibule; here a guard does the check.

detail: only then releases the second door
explain: A vestibule can be fully automated or partly automated, with a guard deciding who moves on. Either way, one door must close before the other opens.

stem: A physical security engineer at a cloud hosting company reviews the door controller settings below for the entry to the server hall.
ask: Which threat are these settings built to stop?

lines: door.inner.unlock   when door.outer = closed and badge = valid

options.why: Door interlocks do nothing against a vehicle; bollards do.
The controller only checks that a badge is valid, so a cloned valid badge would still open the inner door.
Doors that open only one at a time, with one occupant allowed, stop a second person entering on someone else's badge.
Watching someone's screen or PIN is not affected by how the doors open.

detail: door.inner.unlock   when door.outer = closed and badge = valid
explain: Interlocked doors and a one-person occupancy limit are an access control vestibule, which stops tailgating and piggybacking.

stem: An inspection report for an oil refinery lists a "mantrap" at the operations room door. The refinery's facilities planner must record the same item in a standard that uses current terms only.
ask: Which of the following terms should the planner use?

options.why: Video surveillance is cameras, not a two-door entry.
Access control vestibule is the current name for what was called a mantrap.
A pressure sensor is a floor mat or switch, not a room between two doors.
A guard is a person; a mantrap is a two-door space.

detail: lists a "mantrap" at the operations room door
explain: Mantrap is the older name for an access control vestibule; current standards and the exam objectives use the newer name.

stem: The operations manager of a blood bank adds an access control vestibule at the entry to the storage room.
ask: Which of the following statements about the new vestibule are accurate? (Select TWO)

options.t: It keeps vehicles from reaching the building
options.why: Stopping vehicles is the job of bollards outside, not a door space.

options.t: It records video of each person entering
options.why: A vestibule controls passage; recording video is a camera's job.

options.t: It removes the need for any entry check
options.why: Each person is still checked, often with a badge, before the inner door opens.

options.t: Only one of its doors can be open at a time
options.why: The two doors are interlocked so they never stand open together.

options.t: It keeps people from following others inside
options.why: Stopping tailgating and piggybacking is its main job.

detail: at the entry to the storage room
explain: A vestibule has two interlocking doors, only one open at a time, so each person is checked alone and no one follows another in.

ask: Which of the following describes fencing as a physical control?

options.t: A barrier that marks and guards a perimeter
options.why: Fencing marks a boundary and keeps people out of the area inside it.

options.t: Posts that stop vehicles but let walkers pass
options.why: That is bollards, which control vehicles at one frontage.

options.t: Two doors that open only one at a time
options.why: That is an access control vestibule at a single doorway.

options.t: A card that unlocks doors and logs each use
options.why: That is an access badge, used at doors, not along a boundary.

explain: A fence is a perimeter barrier: it marks where the property starts and keeps people out, often as the first layer of physical defense.

ask: Which kind of fence lets guards and cameras watch the grounds on its other side?

options.why: A transparent fence such as mesh or chain link lets people and cameras see through it.
Solid boards are opaque, so they block the view.
A brick wall is opaque and hides what is behind it.
Solid panels are opaque and block the view.

explain: Transparent fences allow visibility through them; opaque ones hide activity on the other side.

stem: The estate manager of a vineyard wants to clearly mark where the private grounds begin. The barrier should also slow down hikers who wander in from the public trail.
ask: Which of the following controls fits this need?

options.why: Bollards stop vehicles and leave gaps for walkers, so hikers would pass straight through.
A fence marks the boundary and delays people on foot crossing it.
A vestibule controls one building door, not the edge of open grounds.
A badge opens doors for staff; it does not mark or guard a boundary.

detail: slow down hikers who wander in from the public trail
explain: Fencing marks a boundary and keeps people out, which is what the vineyard needs along its edge with the trail.

stem: The security manager of an aircraft maker wants drivers on the public road to be unable to see the prototype work in the test yard.
ask: Which of the following should the manager choose for the yard?

options.why: Chain link is transparent, so drivers could still see the work.
Bollards stop vehicles but block no one's view.
An opaque fence hides activity inside from anyone outside.
A camera records the gate; it hides nothing from the road.

detail: unable to see the prototype work
explain: Opaque fences hide what is inside; transparent ones let people see through. The need here is to block the view.

stem: A site supervisor for a water utility finds marks showing that someone climbed the low fence around a pumping station overnight.
ask: Which of the following changes would make the fence harder to cross?

options.t: Replacing it with a see-through mesh
options.why: See-through mesh changes what can be seen, not how hard the fence is to climb.

options.t: Placing steel posts along its base
options.why: Posts at the base stop vehicles, not a person climbing over.

options.t: Putting a camera at the main gate
options.why: A camera at the gate records; it does not stop someone climbing elsewhere.

options.t: Raising it and adding razor wire on top
options.why: Height and razor wire make a fence harder to climb.

detail: someone climbed the low fence
explain: A fence is made harder to climb with more height or with razor wire on top.

stem: The yard manager of a lumber dealer learns that thieves cut through the perimeter fence on a Saturday night. No one knew about it until staff arrived on Monday.
ask: Which of the following explains why the fence did not reveal the break-in?

options.t: A fence detects only people who climb it
options.why: A plain fence detects no one, whether they climb it or cut it.

options.t: A fence works only when it is opaque
options.why: Opaque or transparent changes what can be seen, not whether a breach is reported.

options.t: A fence delays entry but detects nothing
options.why: A fence is a barrier; finding a breach needs cameras, sensors or patrols.

options.t: A fence protects only against vehicles
options.why: Fences are built to keep people out; stopping vehicles is mainly the job of bollards.

detail: No one knew about it until staff arrived on Monday
explain: Fencing is preventive and deterrent, not detective. A breach is noticed only when cameras, sensors or patrols watch the fence line.

stem: The security lead at a water treatment plant needs a perimeter barrier that keeps people out. Guards in the watch tower must still see anyone approaching from outside the barrier.
ask: Which of the following BEST meets both needs?

options.why: A tall transparent fence keeps people out and lets the guards see through it.
A wall keeps people out, but guards cannot see through it.
Bollards leave gaps that people on foot walk through.
A painted line marks a boundary but keeps no one out.

detail: Guards in the watch tower must still see anyone approaching from outside the barrier
edge: The wall keeps people out just as well, but only the transparent fence also lets the tower see through it.
explain: A transparent fence such as chain link keeps people out while guards and cameras can watch the area beyond it.

stem: A physical security consultant hands the facilities manager of a research campus the perimeter specification below.
ask: Which of the following does line P-1 describe?

lines: P-1  3 m welded mesh, anti-climb, topped with barbed tape
P-2  Floodlights on the inside face every 25 m
P-3  Cameras covering the full boundary line
P-4  Two gates, each with a badge reader

options.why: Lighting is line P-2, the floodlights.
Video surveillance is line P-3, the cameras.
Badges are used at the gate readers in line P-4.
Welded anti-climb mesh with barbed tape along the boundary is a fence.

detail: 3 m welded mesh, anti-climb, topped with barbed tape
explain: P-1 is the fence itself, the first layer of the perimeter. The other lines are the lighting, cameras and badge gates that support it.

stem: A security architect at a corporate campus plans that every visitor must arrive through one staffed gate. Along the rest of the boundary, no one should be able to walk in.
ask: Which of the following does the boundary fence do in this plan, besides keeping people out?

options.t: Records who passes through the gate
options.why: A fence records nothing; cameras or badge logs would.

options.t: Funnels all arrivals to one checkpoint
options.why: With the rest of the boundary closed, the fence channels everyone to the gate where they are checked.
Identity checks are done by the guard at the gate, not by the fence.

options.t: Stops vehicles at the lobby doors
options.why: Stopping vehicles at a building front is the job of bollards.

detail: every visitor must arrive through one staffed gate
explain: Fences define the boundary and channel people to controlled gates, where guards, badges or cameras check them.

stem: A broadcast engineer for a radio network has a 3 m anti-climb fence built around a hilltop transmitter mast.
ask: Which of the following control types does the fence provide? (Select TWO)

options.why: A directive control tells people what to do, such as a policy or sign; a fence physically blocks them.
A high anti-climb fence blocks and delays anyone trying to reach the mast.
A clear, hostile barrier discourages people from trying at all.
A fence alone reports nothing; detecting a breach needs cameras, sensors or patrols.
A fence acts before harm and restores nothing afterward.

detail: 3 m anti-climb fence
explain: Fencing is preventive (it blocks and delays) and deterrent (it signals a clear boundary). It is not detective on its own.

ask: Which of the following describes video surveillance?

options.t: Guards who patrol and answer alarms
options.why: That describes security guards, people rather than cameras.

options.t: Cameras that watch and record an area
options.why: Video surveillance is cameras (CCTV) that monitor and record what happens.

options.t: Cards that unlock doors and log entries
options.why: That describes access badges.

options.t: A barrier that marks a site's boundary
options.why: That describes fencing.

explain: Video surveillance uses cameras, often called CCTV (closed-circuit television), to monitor and record areas.

ask: Which of the following is the main job of a camera system in physical security?

options.t: Physically blocking entry to an area
options.why: A camera blocks no one; barriers such as fences and doors do.
Holding people between doors is an access control vestibule.

options.t: Stopping vehicles at a building front
options.why: Stopping vehicles is the job of bollards.
Cameras are mainly detective: they show events live and keep a record.

explain: Video surveillance is mainly a detective control. It does not prevent entry, but it records events and supports investigations.

stem: The owner of a bike repair shop wants a record of who goes into the back storeroom after closing. If stock goes missing again, the record must show the person who took it.
ask: Which of the following controls meets this need?

options.why: Recorded footage shows who entered and supports an investigation of the theft.
A fence around the shop records nothing about who enters a storeroom.
Bollards stop vehicles; they keep no record of people.
A vestibule controls passage one person at a time but keeps no picture of who it was.

detail: the record must show the person who took it
explain: Cameras record who was where, and the recordings support investigations after an incident.

stem: The night manager of a self-storage site wants an alert on his phone whenever anyone moves through the empty corridors. He also wants a clip of each event saved for later.
ask: Which of the following should the manager install?

options.why: Posts stop vehicles; they send no alerts and record nothing.
A fence slows entry but neither alerts on movement nor records it.
Cameras with motion detection send an alert when someone appears and keep the footage.
A booth controls entry at a door; it does not watch the corridors.

detail: a clip of each event saved for later
explain: Modern camera systems add features such as motion detection, which alerts staff and saves footage of what happened.

stem: The property manager of an apartment complex wants a list of the plates of every car that enters the residents' gated lot.
ask: Which of the following provides this list?

options.t: Steel posts at the lot entry
options.why: Posts can keep cars out but cannot read or list plates.
A badge log lists badges used, not the plates of the cars that came in.

options.t: A fence around the whole lot
options.why: A fence keeps people out but records nothing about cars.
Modern cameras can read license plates and record them.

detail: a list of the plates of every car
explain: Video surveillance can include license plate reading, which records the plate of each vehicle that passes a camera.

stem: The loss prevention manager of a home goods chain wants to identify shoplifters after the fact and hand the police recorded evidence of each theft.
ask: Which of the following controls BEST meets this goal?

options.why: A guard may witness a theft, but a witness is not a recording that can be handed over.
Shoppers carry no badges, so badge logs say nothing about them.
Recordings show who took what and can be handed to the police.
A pressure sensor reports weight at one spot and identifies no one.

detail: hand the police recorded evidence
edge: A guard can see a theft happen, but only cameras produce a recording that identifies the person and can be handed to the police.
explain: Camera recordings support investigations: they identify people after the event and serve as evidence.

stem: The operations lead at an airport cargo terminal wants the camera system to flag any bag that is left on the floor unattended for more than 10 minutes.
ask: Which camera feature provides this?

options.why: Motion detection reacts to movement; a bag lying still does not move.
Object detection recognizes items in view, such as a bag left behind.
Facial recognition identifies people by their faces, not bags.
Plate reading identifies vehicles, not items on the floor.

detail: any bag that is left on the floor unattended
explain: Camera analytics include motion detection, object detection, facial recognition and plate reading; a left item is found by object detection.

stem: A security analyst at a fuel distributor exports the event list below from the night of a theft at a depot.
ask: Which control produced these events?

options.why: A camera that detects motion, recognizes a person and stores a clip is video surveillance.
An infrared sensor detects body heat but cannot recognize a person or store a clip.
A pressure sensor reports weight at one spot and stores no images.
A microwave sensor detects movement but records no picture.

detail: cam-03 clip stored case=2211
explain: Only a camera both recognizes what it sees (a person) and stores footage. Sensors raise an alert but keep no images.

stem: The facilities director of a school district wants footage from cameras at 14 schools kept in one place, so that investigators at the district office can search all of it.
ask: Which of the following meets this need?

options.t: Sending all footage to central storage
options.why: Modern systems send footage from many cameras to central storage, where it can be searched.

options.t: Keeping footage on each camera's own card
options.why: Footage left on each camera stays at 14 separate schools.

options.t: Posting a guard at every school entrance
options.why: Guards watch entrances but do not gather footage into one place.

options.t: Issuing badges to every school visitor
options.why: Badges control doors; they do not collect camera footage.

detail: kept in one place
explain: Camera systems can send footage from many cameras to central storage, so one team can review it for investigations.

stem: The operations manager of a gym chain mounts cameras in clear view above each front desk, recording around the clock.
ask: Which of the following control types do these cameras provide? (Select TWO)

options.why: Cameras record events so they can be seen and investigated.
Cameras in clear view discourage wrongdoing by people who see them.
A camera blocks nothing; anyone can still reach the desk.
Cameras restore nothing after an incident.
Nothing in the stem says the cameras stand in for a control that could not be used.

detail: cameras in clear view
explain: Video surveillance is mainly detective, and visible cameras are also deterrent. Cameras do not prevent anything on their own.

ask: Which of the following describes a security guard in physical security?

options.t: A camera that watches and records an area
options.why: That is video surveillance, which records but cannot respond.

options.t: A person who checks access and responds
options.why: A guard checks identities, monitors access, verifies visitors and responds to events.

options.t: A barrier that runs along the property line
options.why: That is fencing, a passive barrier.

options.t: A card that opens only its assigned doors
options.why: That is an access badge, a credential rather than a person.

explain: A security guard is a person who protects a facility by checking identities, monitoring access, verifying visitors and responding to events.

ask: What does two-person integrity require for a sensitive area?

options.t: Two badges issued to every employee
options.why: Extra badges do nothing to stop one person acting alone.

options.t: Two separate fences around the whole site
options.why: A second fence adds a barrier, not a second person watching the first.

options.t: Two authorized people present at once
options.why: Two-person integrity means two authorized people must be present, so no one can act alone.

options.t: Two cameras covering each door at all times
options.why: More cameras record more, but one person could still act alone.

explain: Two-person integrity (the two-person rule) requires at least two authorized people for a sensitive area or task, which reduces insider risk.

stem: The front office manager of an accounting firm reports a visitor at reception who says she is a new contractor. Her name is not on today's visitor list, and she has no letter from the firm.
ask: Which of the following controls can judge this situation and decide what to do?

options.why: Cameras record the visitor but cannot weigh her story or decide anything.
She has no badge, and a badge reader cannot judge an unusual request.
A vestibule admits one checked person at a time; it cannot judge an unlisted visitor's story.
A guard can question her, call the firm and decide whether to admit or escort her.

detail: Her name is not on today's visitor list
explain: Guards are the flexible physical control: they can make judgment calls that machines cannot, such as handling a visitor who is not on the list.

stem: The evidence custodian at a county sheriff's office requires that two authorized officers be present whenever the evidence room is opened.
ask: Which of the following risks does this requirement reduce?

options.t: A car being driven into the room's wall
options.why: Vehicle impacts are stopped by bollards, not by who is in the room.

options.t: Poor camera images in a dark corridor
options.why: Image quality depends on lighting, not on how many people open the room.
With two people present, each can see what the other does, so one insider cannot act unseen.

options.t: A badge being lost on the street
options.why: A lost badge is handled by disabling it; two people at the door do not change that.

detail: two authorized officers be present
explain: This is two-person integrity: requiring two authorized people means no single person can act alone, which reduces insider risk.

stem: The operations director of a television studio wants one control that can check visitors' IDs, escort them to the set, and respond if an alarm sounds.
ask: Which of the following controls can do all three?

options.why: Checking IDs, escorting visitors and responding to alarms are all guard duties.
Cameras can watch, but they cannot check an ID, escort anyone or respond.
Badges open doors; they cannot escort visitors or respond to alarms.
A fence marks the boundary; it does none of the three tasks.

detail: check visitors' IDs, escort them to the set, and respond if an alarm sounds
explain: A guard is the most flexible physical control: one person can verify visitors, monitor access and respond to events.

stem: The IT director of a logistics firm needs a control in the server room corridor that can notice a person behaving oddly and step in to stop them before any harm is done.
ask: Which of the following controls BEST meets this need?

options.why: Cameras can show the person, but they cannot step in to stop anyone.
An infrared sensor senses that a warm body moved, not whether it behaves oddly, and it cannot act.
A badge controls the door; it cannot judge behavior in the corridor.
A guard can notice odd behavior and step in on the spot.

detail: step in to stop them before any harm is done
edge: Cameras can reveal odd behavior, but the need is also to step in before harm, which only a person on site can do.
explain: Guards can judge a situation and act on it at once. Cameras and sensors only detect and record.

stem: The facilities manager of a medical device maker sees that the alarm panel shows door alarms on several nights each month. No one is on site at night, and the alerts are read the next morning.
ask: Which of the following would let an intrusion be dealt with while it is happening?

options.t: Adding more sensors to the doors
options.why: More sensors raise more alerts, but no one is there to act on them.

options.t: Posting a guard who responds at once
options.why: A guard on site can respond to an alarm as it happens.
Lighting helps people and cameras see, but no one is there to respond.

options.t: Recording the alarm panel on camera
options.why: A recording of the panel still waits until morning.

detail: the alerts are read the next morning
explain: Sensors and cameras produce alerts, but someone has to act on them. Guards respond to events in real time.

stem: The site manager of a chemical plant posts the duty sheet below at the gatehouse.
ask: Which control do these duties describe?

lines: 06:00  Walk the fence line and log any damage
08:00  Match contractor IDs to the work permit list
12:00  Watch the camera monitors in the booth
Any time  Answer panel alarms in Building C

options.why: The cameras are something the duty holder watches at noon; they do not patrol or check IDs.
Patrolling, checking IDs, watching monitors and answering alarms are the work of a guard.
A badge is a credential; it performs no duties.
The fence is something the duty holder inspects at 06:00, not the one doing the work.

detail: Match contractor IDs to the work permit list
explain: Guards control entry, monitor cameras and alarms, patrol and respond. A duty sheet like this is written for a guard.

stem: The security manager of a defense contractor learns that a badge stolen from an engineer's car was used to pass the lobby reader. The badge was still valid when it was used.
ask: Which of the following could catch a person using someone else's badge at the lobby?

options.t: A reader that checks the badge is valid
options.why: The stolen badge was valid, so a reader alone lets it through.

options.t: Steel posts outside the lobby doors
options.why: Posts stop vehicles, not a person carrying a badge.

options.t: A fence around the parking area
options.why: A fence along the lot does not check who holds a badge at the lobby.

options.t: A guard matching the photo to the face
options.why: A guard checks the person, not just the card, so a stranger with a stolen badge stands out.

detail: The badge was still valid when it was used
explain: A badge reader authenticates the card, not the person. The photo on a badge is there so a guard can check the person.

stem: The budget committee of a city transit agency debates replacing its night guards with more cameras. The security chief lists what the agency would lose.
ask: Which of the following can a guard do that a camera system cannot? (Select TWO)

options.t: Step in to stop an intruder
options.why: A guard can respond in person; a camera can only record.
Recording is something cameras do, not something they lack.

options.t: Read the plates of passing cars
options.why: Modern cameras can read license plates, so this is not lost.

options.t: Flag movement in a closed area
options.why: Cameras with motion detection already flag movement.

options.t: Make a judgment call on an odd event
options.why: Guards can judge situations no device was set up for.

detail: replacing its night guards with more cameras
explain: Cameras watch, record and flag events, but only a person can judge an unusual situation and respond to it on the spot.

ask: What is an access badge?

options.t: An ID card that unlocks doors
options.why: An access badge is an identification card, often with a photo and an RFID or NFC chip, used to open doors.

options.t: A person who verifies visitors at a desk
options.why: That is a security guard.

options.t: A camera that records who walks past
options.why: That is video surveillance.

options.t: A two-door space that admits one person
options.why: That is an access control vestibule.

explain: An access badge identifies its holder and, presented to a reader, unlocks the doors that holder may use.

ask: Which of the following risks comes with relying on access badges?

options.t: Vehicles driven into the front lobby glass
options.why: That threat is handled by bollards; badges have nothing to do with vehicles.
Climbing a perimeter is a fencing problem, not a badge risk.

options.t: Cards that are lost, shared or cloned
options.why: Whoever holds a lost, shared or copied badge can open the doors it opens.

options.t: Footage that is too dark to use
options.why: Dark footage is a camera and lighting problem, not a badge risk.

explain: A badge is something the holder has, so the main risks are badges that are lost, shared with others or cloned.

stem: The HR director of a software company must find out which doors one employee opened on the night a laptop went missing.
ask: Which of the following records can answer this?

options.why: A fence plan shows the boundary; it records no one's movements.
A drawing of vehicle posts records no door use.
Employees do not sign in as visitors, and the book says nothing about inner doors.
Each badge use is recorded with the badge, door and time, which answers the question.

detail: which doors one employee opened
explain: Badge use can be logged. The usage logs support accounting: they show who opened which door and when.

stem: A facilities coordinator at an engineering firm must remove a departing contractor's access to every door at once. No locks may be changed.
ask: Which of the following should the coordinator do?

options.t: Re-key every lock in the building
options.why: The stem rules out changing locks, and re-keying affects everyone.

options.t: Post a guard at the main entrance
options.why: A guard at one entrance leaves every other door open to the badge.

options.t: Disable the badge in the system
options.why: Disabling one badge centrally removes access to every door without touching any lock.

options.t: Put the contractor's photo at reception
options.why: A photo at reception does nothing at the other doors the badge still opens.

detail: remove a departing contractor's access to every door at once
explain: Electronic badges can be turned off centrally, which removes access everywhere at once, something keys cannot do.

stem: A receptionist at a credit bureau looks at the photo printed on each employee's badge and then at the person holding it.
ask: What is the printed photo on the badge for?

options.t: Unlocking doors through the card reader
options.why: Doors open from the badge's chip, not from the printed photo.

options.t: Letting staff confirm who the holder is
options.why: The photo shows who the badge belongs to, so a person can compare it with the holder.

options.t: Recording each entry in the door log
options.why: The log is written by the reader system, not by the photo.

options.t: Stopping a second person following in
options.why: Stopping a follower is the job of a two-door vestibule.

detail: looks at the photo printed on each employee's badge and then at the person holding it
explain: A badge both shows who someone is (the photo) and opens doors electronically (the chip). The photo is for people to check.

stem: An auditor at a biotech firm shows that a badge dropped in the parking lot lets anyone who picks it up open the lab door.
ask: Which of the following changes would stop a found badge from opening the door by itself?

options.t: Require a code typed in as well
options.why: With a PIN as well, the finder has the card but not the code, so the door stays shut.

options.t: Add a camera above the lab door
options.why: A camera records the finder but still lets the badge open the door.

options.t: Log every use of the badge
options.why: A log records the finder's entry after the fact; the door still opens.

options.t: Print larger photos on all badges
options.why: A photo helps only when a person checks it; the reader ignores it.

detail: lets anyone who picks it up open the lab door
explain: A badge alone is something the holder has. Adding a PIN or biometric means a found badge is not enough.

stem: The property manager of a coworking building lists three requirements for entry to its rented floors.
bullets: Each member opens only the floors they rent
Access ends the day a lease ends, without visiting the doors
A record shows who entered each floor and when
ask: Which of the following BEST meets all three requirements?

options.why: Badges grant per-door rights, are disabled centrally and log every use.
Keys can limit floors, but ending access means collecting keys or changing locks, and keys keep no record.
Cameras record people but do not decide who may open which floor.
A vestibule admits one person at a time but does not set rights per floor.

detail: Access ends the day a lease ends, without visiting the doors
edge: Keys meet the first requirement, but only badges can be turned off centrally and keep a record of each entry.
explain: Badges give rights per door, can be disabled from the system and log every use, so they meet all three requirements.

stem: A security analyst at a research hospital reviews the badge system entries below for one door.
ask: Which of the following do these entries show?

options.t: The badge was copied by an attacker
options.why: Nothing in the log points to a copy; the same badge simply tried at a late hour.

options.t: Late tries were blocked by the time rule
options.why: Both late attempts were denied under the hours rule, and the log recorded them.

options.t: Someone followed the holder into Lab-2
options.why: The log shows badge attempts, not people walking in behind the holder.

options.t: The door was held open after the first entry
options.why: No entry mentions a held door; the late attempts were refused.

detail: DENIED rule=hours
explain: Badge systems check whether a badge may open a door at that time and log every attempt, which lets analysts spot use at unusual hours.

stem: A security analyst at a semiconductor plant finds that one badge tap at the clean room door often lets two or three people in.
ask: Which of the following explains why the badge readers did not stop this?

options.t: The badges must have been cloned
options.why: Only one tap happened; extra people walking in needs no copied badge.

options.t: The readers were not logging any entries at all
options.why: Whether entries are logged does not change who can walk through an open door.

options.t: The readers checked a card, not who walked in
options.why: The reader checks one badge and unlocks; anyone can walk through behind the holder.

options.t: The badges lacked a printed photo
options.why: The reader ignores the photo, so a photo would not stop people following in.

detail: one badge tap at the clean room door often lets two or three people in
explain: Badges do not stop tailgating. An access control vestibule, which admits one checked person at a time, does.

stem: The compliance lead at an investment fund reviews what the records of the badge system can support.
ask: Which of the following can these records support? (Select TWO)

options.t: Proving no one entered without a badge
options.why: A person who follows someone in leaves no badge record at all.

options.t: Naming the person who held a found badge
options.why: The log names the badge, not the person who actually held it.

options.t: Showing whose badge opened the trading room
options.why: Each use is logged with the badge and the door.
Logs with times let reviewers find access outside normal hours.

options.t: Stopping a follower at the door
options.why: Records are written after the fact and stop no one; a vestibule stops followers.

detail: the records of the badge system
explain: Badge logs record which badge opened which door and when. They support accounting and spot odd patterns, but they show badges, not people.

ask: Which of the following describes security lighting?

options.t: Cameras that record activity during the night
options.why: That is video surveillance; lighting helps it but is a separate control.

options.t: Sensors that report body heat in the dark
options.why: That is an infrared sensor, which detects heat rather than lighting an area.

options.t: Posts that keep cars off a walkway after dark
options.why: That is bollards, which stop vehicles at any hour.

options.t: Light that deters intruders and helps cameras
options.why: Security lighting discourages intruders and helps cameras and guards see clearly.

explain: Lighting illuminates outdoor and indoor areas to discourage intruders and to help cameras and guards see.

ask: Which of the following lighting conditions makes camera footage harder to use?

options.t: Even light across the whole area
options.why: Even light is the goal: it removes shadows and helps cameras.

options.t: Lights aimed away from the cameras
options.why: Aiming lights away from lenses avoids glare, which helps footage.
Shadows hide people and glare blinds the camera, so both ruin footage.

options.t: Motion lights that switch on at doors
options.why: A light switching on at movement helps cameras capture the person.

explain: Good lighting is even, with no deep shadows and no glare into camera lenses, so footage stays usable.

stem: The security manager of a furniture maker reviews the cameras in its rear yard, which record clearly by day. At night the footage is too dark to identify anyone.
ask: Which of the following would fix the night footage?

options.t: Brighter, even lighting in the yard
options.why: More even light lets the existing cameras capture usable images at night.

options.t: Additional cameras in the same yard
options.why: More cameras in the dark still record unusable images.

options.t: A taller fence around the yard
options.why: A taller fence slows intruders but does nothing for image quality.

options.t: Badge readers on the yard gates
options.why: Badge readers control the gates but do not light the yard.

detail: At night the footage is too dark to identify anyone
explain: Lighting improves camera image quality. When footage is too dark, the fix is light, not more cameras.

stem: The owner of a marina wants would-be thieves walking along the docks at night to feel exposed and decide to leave.
ask: Which of the following controls fits this aim?

options.why: Bollards stop vehicles; people on foot walk past them unseen in the dark.
A vestibule controls a building door, not open docks.
An infrared sensor detects body heat quietly; an intruder does not feel exposed by it.
Bright light makes intruders feel seen, which discourages them.

detail: feel exposed and decide to leave
explain: Lighting is a deterrent: an intruder who feels exposed is more likely to give up.

stem: The security lead of a wildlife park must record the outer paddocks at night. Bright lights are not allowed there because they would disturb the animals.
ask: Which of the following meets this need?

options.why: The stem rules out bright lights in the paddocks.
Infrared cameras can work in low light, so the paddocks are recorded without bright lights.
A fence marks the boundary; it records nothing.
Badges control the gates; they record nothing inside the paddocks.

detail: Bright lights are not allowed there
explain: Infrared cameras can work in low light, which helps where lighting cannot be added.

stem: A stone quarry's site manager has new floodlights pointed straight at the cameras in the equipment yard. Since then the night footage shows mostly white bloom.
ask: Which of the following explains why the footage got worse?

options.t: Light that is too even confuses cameras
options.why: Even light helps cameras; it is the aim of good lighting.

options.t: Glare from the lights is blinding the cameras
options.why: Light shining into a lens washes out the image; fixtures should be aimed at the area, not the cameras.

options.t: Cameras cannot record under artificial light
options.why: Cameras record well under artificial light that is aimed properly.

options.t: Brighter areas make cameras switch off
options.why: Cameras do not switch off in light; the problem is the light pointing into the lens.

detail: pointed straight at the cameras
explain: More light is not always better. Glare can blind cameras and guards, so lights are aimed to light the area without shining into lenses.

stem: The caretaker of a church wants the side door lit only when someone comes near it, so that the light switching on draws attention to the person.
ask: Which of the following meets this need?

options.t: A light left on all night
options.why: A light that is always on cannot draw attention by switching on.
A camera records and alerts, but it does not light the door.

options.t: An infrared sensor on the alarm
options.why: An infrared sensor can trigger an alarm, but it gives no light.
It stays off until movement, and switching on draws attention to whoever approached.

detail: lit only when someone comes near it
explain: Motion-activated lights are used where constant light is not needed; the light coming on draws attention to movement.

stem: A physical security assessor gives the facilities manager of a print shop the night lighting findings below.
ask: Which of the following fixes the staff lot finding?

lines: North gate    two fixtures working, even coverage
Loading bay   one fixture failed, dark gap between cam-4 and cam-5
Staff lot     lights shine directly into the cam-9 lens
Front walk    motion light at the side door working

options.t: Aim the lights away from the lens
options.why: Light shining into a lens is glare; aiming the fixtures at the area instead fixes it.

options.t: Add more lights to the lot
options.why: More light shining at the lens makes the glare worse, not better.

options.t: Add a second camera beside cam-9
options.why: A second camera beside it would face the same glare.

options.t: Switch the lot to motion lighting
options.why: Motion lights would still shine into the lens whenever they are on.

detail: lights shine directly into the cam-9 lens
explain: Lighting must avoid both shadows and glare. Shadows need more light; glare needs fixtures aimed away from cameras and guards.

stem: Cameras watch the rear boundary of a recycling depot, but the area is dark at night. The guard in the gate booth also cannot see anyone approaching along it.
ask: Which of the following would BEST help both the cameras and the guard?

options.why: Infrared cameras can record in low light, but they do not help the guard see.
A taller fence slows intruders but leaves the area just as dark.
Light helps cameras record clearly and lets the guard see the boundary.
Mats report weight at one spot; they help neither the cameras nor the guard see.

detail: The guard in the gate booth also cannot see anyone approaching
edge: Infrared cameras solve the camera side alone; lighting helps both cameras and guards see, which the stem asks for.
explain: Lighting supports both cameras and guards, which is why it is one of the cheapest controls that improves several others at once.

stem: The town manager of a seaside resort has new lighting installed along the service lane behind its shops.
ask: Which of the following benefits does the new lighting bring? (Select TWO)

options.t: It physically blocks entry to the shops
options.why: Light blocks no one; barriers and locks do that.

options.t: It records who walks past at night
options.why: Lights record nothing; cameras do.

options.t: It stops vehicles reaching the shop fronts
options.why: Stopping vehicles is the job of bollards.

options.t: It discourages people planning a break-in
options.why: Intruders who feel seen are more likely to give up.
Better light means usable images at night.

detail: new lighting along the service lane
explain: Lighting is a deterrent and improves camera image quality. It does not block entry or record anything itself.

ask: Which of the following describes sensors used in physical security?

options.t: Barriers that physically stop people getting in
options.why: Stopping people is the job of barriers such as fences and doors, not sensors.

options.t: Cards that identify people at doors
options.why: That describes access badges.

options.t: Cameras that send footage to central storage
options.why: That describes video surveillance.

options.t: Devices that detect a change and send an alert
options.why: Sensors detect a change such as heat, weight, movement or sound and trigger an alert.

explain: A sensor detects a physical change (heat, weight, movement, sound) and triggers an alert.

source.chapter: Infrared vs pressure vs microwave vs ultrasonic sensors (physical sensors compared)

ask: Which of the following happens when an intrusion sensor is triggered?

options.t: It locks the door the intruder came through
options.why: A sensor does not lock anything; it detects and reports.

options.t: It puts the area back to how it was
options.why: Restoring things after an incident is corrective work, not what a sensor does.

options.t: It reports the change so someone can act
options.why: Sensors are detective: they raise an alert about what they sensed.

options.t: It shows the intruder a written warning
options.why: A sensor does not display warnings; it alerts the people watching.

explain: Sensors are detective controls. They notice a physical change and trigger an alert so that someone can respond.

source.chapter: Infrared vs pressure vs microwave vs ultrasonic sensors (physical sensors compared)

stem: An alarm installer for a florist explains the shop's three devices. One in the cold room reacts to heat, one at the back door reacts to weight, and one in the hall reacts to reflected waves.
ask: Which of the following do all three devices have in common?

options.why: None of them blocks anyone; they only sense.

options.t: They detect a change and raise an alert
options.why: Each one senses a different change, but all of them detect and alert.

options.t: They record video of the intruder
options.why: None of them records images; cameras do that.

options.t: They identify who the intruder is
options.why: None of them identifies a person; they report that something changed.

detail: reacts to heat, one at the back door reacts to weight, and one in the hall reacts to reflected waves
explain: Infrared, pressure and motion sensors sense different things, but all are detective: they detect a physical change and trigger an alert.

source.chapter: Infrared vs pressure vs microwave vs ultrasonic sensors (physical sensors compared)

stem: The manager of a coin dealer has a thin mat hidden under the rug in front of the safe as part of the alarm system.
ask: Which physical change does the mat respond to?

options.why: A mat under a rug senses the weight of someone stepping on it.
Heat is sensed by infrared sensors, not by a floor mat.
Echoes of sound are used by ultrasonic sensors, not mats.
A mat under a rug senses nothing about light.

detail: a thin mat hidden under the rug
explain: A floor mat is a pressure sensor: it detects weight, while infrared detects heat and microwave and ultrasonic detect movement.

source.chapter: Infrared vs pressure vs microwave vs ultrasonic sensors (physical sensors compared)

stem: A technician at an alarm company tells a trainee that two of the sensors she installs send out waves and watch for changes in what bounces back.
ask: Which physical change do these two sensors detect?

options.why: Changes in the reflected waves show that something moved.
Weight is detected by a pressure sensor, which sends out no waves.
Body heat is detected by an infrared sensor, which sends out nothing.
None of the reflected-wave sensors measure light.

detail: send out waves and watch for changes in what bounces back
explain: Microwave and ultrasonic sensors detect movement by reflected waves: radio waves for microwave, sound for ultrasonic.

source.chapter: Infrared vs pressure vs microwave vs ultrasonic sensors (physical sensors compared)

stem: The facilities manager of a bakery supply warehouse sees many false alarms from one motion sensor near warm ovens. The installer offers a unit that raises an alarm only when its heat sensing and its microwave sensing both trigger.
ask: Which of the following describes the offered unit?

options.why: A plain infrared detector senses heat alone, which is what the ovens set off.
A detector that pairs two sensing methods and alarms only when both trigger is dual-technology.
A plain microwave sensor uses one method and alarms on its own.
A mat senses weight and uses neither heat nor microwaves.

detail: only when its heat sensing and its microwave sensing both trigger
explain: A dual-technology detector pairs infrared with microwave or ultrasonic and alarms only when both agree, which cuts false alarms.

source.chapter: Infrared vs pressure vs microwave vs ultrasonic sensors (physical sensors compared)

stem: The security lead of a pharmacy needs to detect movement anywhere in the dispensary at night. One wall of the dispensary is glass, facing the shop floor where cleaners work.
ask: Which of the following sensor types fit this need? (Select TWO)

options.why: A door contact reports a door opening, not movement anywhere in the room.
Infrared covers the room and does not sense through glass, so cleaners outside do not trigger it.

options.why: A pressure sensor reacts to force or weight applied to a surface.

options.t: A sensor that reads echoes of high-pitched sound

stem: A records manager at a title insurance company wants an alert when anyone steps just inside the file room door. Tall shelving blocks any clear view of that spot from the walls and ceiling.

Ultrasonic fills a room with sound and reacts to movement anywhere in it.

options.why: Both are active: each sends out a signal and reads its echoes.

options.t: Ultrasonic passes walls, microwave stays inside
options.why: It is the other way round: microwave passes light walls and ultrasonic stays inside.

detail: both offer motion detectors that read returning echoes
explain: Ultrasonic and microwave sensors both detect motion from echoes. Ultrasonic uses sound; microwave uses radio waves, which pass through light walls.

stem: The owner of a hardware store reads the manual for the new ultrasonic sensor in the key-cutting room.
ask: Which of the following statements about the sensor are accurate? (Select TWO)

options.t: It works only while the lights are on
options.why: Sound needs no light, so it works in the dark.

options.t: It sends out sound above human hearing
options.why: Ultrasonic means sound beyond what people can hear.

options.t: Its sound does not pass through the walls
options.why: The sound stays inside the room.

options.t: It detects people by their body heat
options.why: Body heat is what infrared senses.

options.t: It reads changes in radio reflections
options.why: Radio reflections are what microwave sensors read.

detail: the new ultrasonic sensor in the key-cutting room
explain: An ultrasonic sensor emits sound beyond human hearing, detects motion by echo changes and stays within the room it watches.

ask: Which of the following describes deception and disruption technology?

options.t: Rules that block known attack traffic at the edge
options.why: Blocking known traffic is a filtering control, not a decoy.

options.t: Decoys that lure attackers and reveal their methods
options.why: Decoy systems and data draw attackers in, waste their time and show how they work.

options.t: Copies of real data kept for recovery after loss
options.why: Keeping copies for recovery is backup, which lures no one.

options.t: Checks that prove who a user is before sign-in
options.why: Proving identity is authentication, not deception.

explain: Deception and disruption technology uses decoys (honeypots, honeynets, honeyfiles, honeytokens) to lure attackers, waste their time and reveal their methods.

ask: Which of the following explains why any contact with a decoy is treated as suspicious?

options.t: Decoys hold the most valuable real data
options.why: Decoys hold fake data; nothing real is stored on them.

options.t: Decoys block every attacker on contact
options.why: Decoys detect and divert; they do not block attackers.

options.t: Decoys are placed only outside the network
options.why: Decoys can sit inside the network too, to catch intruders moving around.

options.t: No legitimate user has a reason to touch it
options.why: A decoy serves no business purpose, so whoever touches it is suspect.

explain: Any interaction with a decoy is suspicious by definition, because no normal work ever touches it.

stem: The chief information security officer of a regional airline has the team set up a fake file server, fake documents and fake access keys, then watch for anyone who touches them.
ask: Which of the following is a goal of these decoys?

options.why: Watching what attackers do with the decoys reveals their tools and methods.

options.t: Stopping every attack on real systems
options.why: Decoys detect and divert; they do not stop attacks on real systems.
Decoys hold fake data and encrypt nothing.

options.t: Backing up the real file servers
options.why: Backups protect real data; decoys are fake by design.

detail: watch for anyone who touches them
explain: Deception technology is used to learn attacker techniques and to detect intrusions, since only an intruder touches a decoy.

options.why: Nothing in the stem concerns encryption.
Proving who sent a message is non-repudiation, not a decoy benefit.
The decoys kept the intruders busy for two days, which is the disruption side of deception.
Restoring data is recovery; the decoys held no real data.

explain: Decoys lure attackers and waste their time, and meanwhile they reveal their methods.

ask: Which of the following flash cards is accurate?

options.why: A honeypot is a decoy system, not a document.
A honeyfile is one decoy file, not a network.
A honeytoken is a piece of traceable data, not a server.
A honeynet is a whole network of decoys.

detail: the four kinds of decoy
explain: Pot = a system, net = a network of systems, file = a document, token = a piece of traceable data.

stem: A board member at a marine insurer asks whether the new decoy servers will stop attacks on the real claims servers.
ask: Which of the following answers the question?

options.t: Yes, they block any attacker who touches them
options.why: Touching a decoy raises an alert; it does not block the attacker.

options.t: Yes, they encrypt the real servers' data
options.why: Decoys do nothing to the real servers' data.

options.t: No, they detect and divert but block nothing
options.why: Decoys are detective: they reveal and distract attackers but do not stop attacks on real systems.

options.t: No, they work only after data is sold
options.why: Decoy servers alert on first contact, long before any data could be sold.

detail: will stop attacks on the real claims servers
explain: Deception tools are detective, not preventive. They detect and divert attackers, so they work alongside the controls that block attacks.

source.chapter: Honeypot vs honeynet vs honeyfile vs honeytoken (deception technologies compared)

stem: A security architect at a hospital network wants alerts about intruders moving inside the network, and the alerts must have almost no false positives.
ask: Which of the following BEST meets this requirement?

options.why: An IDS detects intrusions too, but it judges ordinary traffic, so some alerts are false.
No normal traffic ever goes to a decoy, so its alerts are high confidence with few false positives.
Cameras watch physical spaces, not movement inside a network.
Badge logs record doors opened, not intruders on the network.

detail: the alerts must have almost no false positives
edge: An IDS also detects intruders, but it alerts on patterns in everyday traffic; any contact with a decoy is suspicious, which keeps false positives near zero.
explain: Decoys give unusually reliable alerts because no legitimate activity should ever touch them.

options.why: The decoy has no business users, so any login attempt on it comes from an intruder.

options.why: A decoy holds fake data, not real records.

options.t: The login attempt on the decoy succeeded
options.why: The alert reports an attempt, not a success; the attempt alone is enough.

options.t: The decoy blocked the host from the network
options.why: Decoys do not block; this one only raised an alert.

stem: The security manager of a design agency wants to know whether anyone is browsing the shared project folders looking for something valuable. No real files may be changed.
ask: Which kind of decoy fits this need?

options.why: A tempting fake file in the folders alerts when someone opens it, which shows browsing.
A honeynet shows movement between decoy systems, not reading of shared folders.
A honeypot is a whole decoy system; the need is about the existing shared folders.
A honeytoken alerts when fake data is used elsewhere, not when a folder is browsed.

explain: To know whether someone is reading sensitive folders, place a honeyfile there; it alerts on access.

stem: A new security operations analyst at a game studio reads the team's deception runbook.
ask: Which of the following statements in the runbook are accurate? (Select TWO)

options.t: Any contact with a decoy is suspicious
options.why: No normal work touches a decoy.
Watching activity on decoys shows how attackers work.

options.t: Decoys prevent attacks on real systems
options.why: Decoys are detective; they do not stop attacks elsewhere.

options.t: Decoys must hold real data to work
options.why: Decoys hold fake data by design.

options.t: Decoys need no isolation from production
options.why: Decoy systems are isolated so a captured decoy cannot reach real systems.

explain: Decoys are detective: any contact is suspicious and reveals attacker methods. They hold fake data and are isolated from real systems.

ask: Which of the following describes a honeypot?

options.t: A network of several linked decoy systems
options.why: Several linked decoys form a honeynet, not a single honeypot.

options.t: One decoy system made to look like a real target
options.why: A honeypot is a single decoy system that looks valuable, built to attract and study attackers.

options.t: A fake document that alerts when it is opened
options.why: A decoy document is a honeyfile, not a system.

options.t: A fake credential that alerts when it is used
options.why: A decoy credential is a honeytoken, a piece of data rather than a system.

explain: A honeypot is a single decoy system that looks like a real, valuable target, so attackers who touch it can be watched and studied.

ask: Which of the following does a honeypot normally hold?

options.t: A live copy of production data
options.why: Real data on a decoy would put it at risk; a honeypot holds none.
Real customer records never belong on a decoy.

options.t: Fake data that only looks valuable
options.why: A honeypot looks like a valuable target but holds no real data.
Backups are real data and belong on protected systems, not a decoy.

explain: A honeypot is a decoy: it is built to look valuable, but nothing on it is real, so attackers can be studied without risk to real data.

stem: A network engineer at a regional bank sets up one fake server that looks like an old payment gateway. It holds no real data, and every connection to it is recorded.
ask: Which of the following is the engineer's goal?

options.t: Serving real customers at busy times
options.why: It holds no real data and serves no customers.

options.t: Keeping a spare copy of the gateway
options.why: A spare copy would hold real data; this server is fake.
A decoy records attackers; it does not block them.
A decoy that records every connection lets the team watch what attackers do.

detail: every connection to it is recorded
explain: A honeypot attracts attackers so their activity can be watched and studied; it holds nothing real.

stem: A security analyst at a logistics firm has run one decoy server for a year. The CISO (chief information security officer) now wants several decoy servers, workstations and a router linked to look like a branch office.
ask: Which of the following has the analyst been running for the past year?

options.why: A honeynet is what the CISO now wants: many linked decoys.
The analyst runs a server, not a file.
One decoy server on its own is a honeypot.
The analyst runs a server, not a planted credential.

detail: run one decoy server for a year
explain: A honeypot is one decoy system; a honeynet is many decoys working together.

stem: A penetration tester hired by a pharmacy chain finds a server named "trap-01" that runs default settings and carries no traffic at all. She ignores it and moves on.
ask: Which honeypot weakness does this show?

options.t: A poorly built decoy can be spotted
options.why: An obvious name, default settings and no traffic gave the decoy away.

options.t: A decoy blocks testers from real servers
options.why: Nothing was blocked; the tester simply skipped the decoy.

options.t: A decoy exposes real customer records
options.why: The decoy holds no real records.

options.t: A decoy can only sit outside the network
options.why: Decoys can sit inside the network; placement is not the problem here.

detail: runs default settings and carries no traffic at all
explain: Attackers may recognize a poor honeypot. A decoy needs a believable name, settings and activity to work.

stem: A junior administrator at a game publisher plans to put a honeypot on the same flat network as the production database, with open routes between them.
ask: Which of the following is the main risk of this placement?

options.t: The honeypot would raise too few alerts
options.why: Placement next to production does not reduce the decoy's alerts.

options.t: Every login would need legal approval
options.why: Legal review may be needed for a honeypot, but not for each login, and it is not the risk of this placement.

options.t: The decoy would slow database queries
options.why: A separate decoy does not slow the real database.

options.t: An attacker could use it to reach real systems
options.why: Without isolation, an attacker who takes over the decoy can launch attacks on production.

detail: with open routes between them
explain: A honeypot must be isolated so that an attacker who takes it over cannot use it as a launch point against real systems.

stem: The security lead of a city government wants to know whether attackers inside the network are scanning servers and trying to log in to them. The budget covers only one decoy system, physical or virtual.
ask: Which of the following should the security lead deploy?

options.why: A honeynet needs several decoy systems, even when they run as virtual machines, more than the budget covers.
One decoy system alerts on any scan or login attempt against it.
A decoy file shows folder browsing, not scans and logins against servers.
A honeytoken shows fake data being used, not servers being scanned.

detail: The budget covers only one decoy system
explain: To learn whether someone is probing or attacking systems, use a honeypot; a honeynet needs many decoys.
