stem: A security analyst at a frozen food maker reads the entries below from a decoy database server.
ask: Which of the following can the team learn from these entries?

options.t: Which real database the attacker breached
options.why: trap-sql01 is a decoy; no real database appears.

options.t: The attacker's address and the tool brought in
options.why: The decoy recorded where the connection came from and the program uploaded.

options.t: Where stolen data was later offered for sale
options.why: Tracing data after it leaves is what honeytokens do.

options.t: Which shared folder the attacker opened
options.why: Folder access is what a honeyfile reports; no folder appears here.

detail: file upload tool.exe 412 KB
explain: A honeypot logs scans, logins, commands and uploaded tools, so defenders learn attacker addresses and techniques.

stem: A threat researcher at a university places a honeypot so that it faces the internet directly.
ask: Which of the following will this placement mainly show?

options.why: Lateral movement is caught by decoys inside the network, ideally a honeynet.
Folder browsing is shown by honeyfiles on internal shares.
Use of stolen data is shown by honeytokens.
An internet-facing decoy collects scans and attacks from outside.

detail: faces the internet directly
explain: A honeypot can sit inside the network to catch lateral movement or face the internet to study attack traffic.

stem: The IT director of a cosmetics company asks the security team what a planned honeypot will and will not do.
ask: Which of the following statements about the honeypot are accurate? (Select TWO)

options.t: It must be isolated from real systems
options.why: Isolation stops a captured decoy from attacking production.
A honeypot holds only fake data.

options.t: It blocks attacks on production servers
options.why: It detects and diverts; it does not block attacks elsewhere.

options.t: It shows where stolen files end up
options.why: Tracing where data ends up is what honeytokens do.

options.t: It gives alerts with very few false positives
options.why: Normal traffic never goes to a decoy, so its alerts are high confidence.

detail: a planned honeypot
explain: A honeypot gives high-confidence alerts because no one legitimate touches it, and it must be isolated from real systems.

ask: Which of the following describes a honeynet?

options.t: Several linked decoys that imitate a real network
options.why: A honeynet is a network of honeypots and other decoys that together look like a real environment.

options.t: One decoy server built to look valuable
options.why: A single decoy server is a honeypot.

options.t: A fake document placed on a file share
options.why: A decoy document is a honeyfile.

options.t: A fake access key planted in source code
options.why: A planted fake key is a honeytoken.

explain: A honeynet is a network of multiple honeypots and other decoy resources (servers, workstations, routers) that imitate a real environment.

ask: What can a honeynet show that a single honeypot cannot?

options.t: A first scan against one exposed system
options.why: A single honeypot already shows a first scan.

options.t: Where stolen records end up later on
options.why: Tracing stolen data is what honeytokens do.

options.t: An attacker moving from system to system
options.why: With several connected decoys, defenders watch the attacker move laterally between them.

options.t: Who opened a decoy document on a share
options.why: Opening a decoy document is what a honeyfile reports.

explain: A honeynet shows lateral movement, which one decoy system cannot show.

stem: Researchers at a university security lab want to watch how intruders move from a mail server to a payroll server and then to a backup server. No real systems may be put at risk.
ask: Which of the following should the researchers build?

options.why: One decoy system cannot show movement from one server to another.
A decoy file shows that someone opened it, not movement between servers.
A decoy credential shows that it was used, not the path across servers.
Several connected decoy servers let them watch the intruder move between systems.

detail: move from a mail server to a payroll server and then to a backup server
explain: A honeynet is many decoys together, so it shows lateral movement; a single honeypot cannot.

stem: A deception engineer at an energy trader sees skilled attackers quickly leave a lone decoy server. She adds decoy workstations, a fake router and realistic traffic around it.
ask: Which of the following is the main gain from this change?

options.t: Real data for attackers to take
options.why: Every added system is a decoy; nothing real is added.
There are now more decoy systems, all of which must stay isolated.
A whole decoy network looks more like a real environment than one server alone.

options.t: A lower cost than one decoy
options.why: Several decoys cost more than one, not less.

detail: skilled attackers quickly leave a lone decoy server
explain: A honeynet is more convincing than a single honeypot and shows lateral movement, which is why it is worth its extra cost.

stem: A department head at a software reseller asks whether the company's new honeynet includes any of its real servers.
ask: Which of the following answers the question?

options.t: Yes, it includes the real web servers
options.why: Real servers are never part of a honeynet.

options.t: No, every system in it is a decoy
options.why: A honeynet is built only from decoy resources.

options.t: Yes, one real server anchors the rest
options.why: Even one real server would put real data at risk; none is included.

options.t: No, it is just one fake document
options.why: A honeynet is a network of decoy systems, not a single document.

detail: includes any of its real servers
explain: A honeynet is a network of honeypots and other decoys; it imitates a real environment without containing one.

stem: A new network administrator at a magazine publisher confuses the company's honeynet with its screened subnet, where the public website runs.
ask: Which of the following describes the difference?

options.t: Only the honeynet consists entirely of decoys
options.why: A screened subnet holds real public services; a honeynet holds only decoys.

options.t: Only the honeynet can face the internet
options.why: A screened subnet faces the internet too; that is where the public website runs.

options.t: Only the screened subnet records attackers
options.why: Recording attacker activity is the main job of the honeynet.

options.t: Only the screened subnet must be isolated
options.why: A honeynet must be isolated from production as well.

detail: where the public website runs
explain: A honeynet is not a screened subnet: the screened subnet holds real public services, while the honeynet holds only decoys.

stem: An incident response lead at an online broker wants to capture an attacker's full path across several systems: discovery, credential theft and movement between machines.
ask: Which of the following BEST meets this goal?

options.why: Several connected decoys let the team watch the attacker move from machine to machine.
A honeypot captures first contact with one system, but not movement across several.
A honeyfile shows that a file was opened, not a path across systems.
A honeytoken shows that fake data was used, not the path the attacker took.

detail: full path across several systems
edge: A honeypot also catches the attacker, but only at one system; the goal is the path across several, which needs a network of decoys.
explain: A honeynet shows the full attack path, including lateral movement, which a single honeypot cannot.

stem: A security engineer at a furniture retailer shares the deception design below with the IT manager.
ask: Which of the following does this design describe?

lines: segment:  isolated, no route to production
capture:  full packets and commands on every decoy

Three connected decoy systems on an isolated segment form a honeynet.
A honeyfile is one decoy file, not connected systems.
A screened subnet holds real public services; this segment holds only decoys.

stem: The architect of a honeynet at a car rental company places it on a segment with no route to the production network.
ask: Which of the following explains this placement?

options.why: The honeynet must still be found by attackers to be useful.
Isolation is about safety, not speed.

options.t: Malware brought in cannot reach real systems
options.why: Isolation keeps anything an attacker drops on the decoys away from production.

options.t: The honeynet then needs no logging
options.why: Every decoy is still fully logged; that is the point of a honeynet.

detail: no route to the production network
explain: The whole honeynet is isolated from production so that malicious code brought in by an attacker cannot spread from the decoys to real systems.

stem: A budget review at a satellite operator compares a planned honeynet with the single honeypot the team runs today.
ask: Which of the following statements about the honeynet are accurate? (Select TWO)

options.t: It runs real services for customers
options.why: A honeynet holds only decoys.

options.t: It needs no isolation from production
options.why: A honeynet must be isolated so attackers cannot spread from it.

options.t: It costs more to build and keep believable
options.why: More decoys mean more work to keep them convincing.

options.t: It can run as virtual machines on one host
options.why: A honeynet can be virtual, with the whole fake network on one physical host.

options.t: It shows only an attacker's first contact
options.why: First contact is what a single honeypot shows; a honeynet also shows movement.

detail: a planned honeynet
explain: A honeynet is costlier and more convincing than one honeypot, can be virtual on one host, and must be isolated from production.

ask: Which of the following describes a honeyfile?

options.t: Fake data that alerts when it is used elsewhere
options.why: Traceable data that alerts when used is a honeytoken.

options.t: One decoy system that draws attackers in
options.why: A decoy system is a honeypot.

options.t: A network of linked decoy systems
options.why: A network of decoys is a honeynet.

options.t: A decoy file that raises an alert when accessed
options.why: A honeyfile is a tempting fake file; any access to it triggers an alert.

explain: A honeyfile is a decoy file with an attractive name and fake contents; any access to it triggers an alert.

ask: What sets off the alert of a honeyfile?

options.t: Someone logging in to a decoy server
options.why: A login to a decoy server is a honeypot alert.
Movement between decoys is what a honeynet shows.

options.t: Someone opening or copying the file
options.why: A honeyfile alerts on access, such as opening, copying or moving it.

options.t: Someone stepping on a hidden floor mat
options.why: A floor mat is a pressure sensor, a physical control.

explain: The honeyfile itself is the bait: whoever opens, copies or moves it sets off the alert.

stem: A file named "board-salaries-2027.xlsx" sits on the finance share of a cement maker. It holds made-up figures, and each time it is opened a message goes to security.
ask: Which of the following is this file?

options.why: A tempting file with fake contents that alerts when opened is a honeyfile.
A honeytoken alerts when a piece of fake data is used, not when a file is opened.
A honeypot is a whole decoy system, not one file.
A honeynet is a network of decoy systems.

detail: each time it is opened a message goes to security
explain: A honeyfile is bait: a file with an attractive name and fake contents that alerts whenever someone opens it.

stem: The IT manager of a law firm sees an alert: a paralegal opened "partner-bonuses.docx", a decoy that no task at the firm requires.
ask: Which of the following does this alert show?

options.t: The firm's real bonus data was stolen
options.why: The file is a decoy with fake contents; no real data was in it.

options.t: An attacker used a fake password elsewhere
options.why: Use of fake data elsewhere is a honeytoken alert; here a file was opened.

options.t: A decoy server was attacked from the internet
options.why: An attack on a decoy server is a honeypot alert; here a file was opened.

options.t: Someone browsed for data they did not need
options.why: No task needs the decoy, so opening it shows someone looking where they should not.

detail: a decoy that no task at the firm requires
explain: Because staff never need a honeyfile, any access to it is a strong sign of an intruder or a curious insider.

stem: After a honeyfile is placed on the HR share, a manager at a staffing agency says the real HR files on that share are now protected from theft.
ask: Which of the following corrects the manager?

options.t: The decoy encrypts the real files on the share
options.why: A decoy changes nothing about the real files.

options.t: The decoy detects browsing but protects nothing
options.why: A honeyfile raises an alert when touched; it does not guard the real files beside it.

options.t: The decoy blocks anyone who opens a real file
options.why: A honeyfile blocks no one; it only alerts when it is itself accessed.

options.t: The decoy moves real files to a safe place
options.why: A decoy moves nothing; the real files stay where they are.

detail: the real HR files on that share are now protected from theft
explain: A honeyfile is detective. It reveals someone browsing before real data leaves, but it does not protect the real files.

stem: The security lead of a biotech firm wants an alert the moment anyone opens a tempting spreadsheet on the research share, whether or not anything inside it is ever used later.
ask: Which of the following BEST meets this goal?

options.why: A honeytoken is planted data whose use or sighting raises the alert; the goal is an alert on opening the file itself.
A honeyfile alerts on access, so opening the spreadsheet is enough.
A honeypot is a decoy system; the need is about one file on a real share.
A honeynet is a network of decoy systems, not a file on a share.

detail: the moment anyone opens a tempting spreadsheet
edge: Fake data planted inside the spreadsheet is a honeytoken and alerts when that data is used or seen; an alert on opening the file is the defining trigger of a honeyfile.
explain: A honeyfile alerts when it is accessed; a honeytoken alerts when its data is used or shows up somewhere.

stem: A security engineer at a city council must make a decoy file raise an alert when it is opened. The file server it sits on runs no monitoring agent.
ask: Which of the following could provide the alert?

options.t: A pressure mat under the file server
options.why: A mat senses weight on the floor, not a file being opened.

options.t: A camera aimed at the server rack
options.why: A camera watches the rack, not files opened over the network.

options.t: Renaming the file once a week
options.why: Renaming changes the bait but raises no alert.

options.t: Content in the file that calls back on access
options.why: A remote image or link inside the file contacts a monitor when the file is opened.

detail: The file server it sits on runs no monitoring agent
explain: A honeyfile can be watched by file auditing, a monitoring agent, or content in the file that calls back when it is opened.

stem: A security analyst at a mediation firm finds the audit event below on the file server. The file is a decoy.
ask: Which of the following explains why this event is a strong sign of an intruder?

options.t: No legitimate task ever needs that file
options.why: Staff and services never need the decoy, so any access to it is suspicious.

options.t: Spreadsheets are opened only by attackers
options.why: Staff open real spreadsheets all the time; it is this decoy that no one should open.

options.t: Service accounts are never allowed to read files
options.why: Services read files as part of their work; the decoy is what makes this suspicious.

options.t: The file holds the firm's real settlements
options.why: The stem says the file is a decoy with nothing real in it.

detail: The file is a decoy
explain: A honeyfile gives very few false alarms because no one needs it, so an access like this one is investigated at once.

stem: The deception lead at a regional newspaper wants honeyfiles to catch an intruder who is hunting through the network for something valuable.
ask: Where should the honeyfiles be placed?

options.t: On an isolated server no one can reach
options.why: A file no one can reach will never be opened by the intruder either.

options.t: On the public website for download
options.why: Public downloads would bring alerts from anyone online, not only the intruder.

options.t: On file shares and admin desktops
options.why: An intruder hunting for valuables browses shares and admin machines, so the bait belongs there.

options.t: Only on the security team's own laptops
options.why: Placing them only there leaves the shares and admin machines the intruder searches without any bait.

detail: hunting through the network for something valuable
explain: Honeyfiles are placed where an attacker would look: file shares, admin desktops and similar places.

stem: A security trainer at a telecom company prepares a slide comparing honeyfiles with honeytokens.
ask: Which of the following statements belong on the slide? (Select TWO)

options.t: A honeyfile alerts only when its data is sold
options.why: A honeyfile alerts on access; sightings of data elsewhere are a honeytoken trait.

options.t: A honeytoken is always a whole document
options.why: A honeytoken is a piece of data such as a key or record, not a whole file.

options.t: A honeyfile protects the real files near it
options.why: A honeyfile detects browsing; it protects nothing.

options.t: A honeyfile alerts when it is opened
options.why: Access to the file is the trigger.

options.t: A honeytoken alerts when its data is used
options.why: Use or sighting of the fake data is the trigger.

detail: comparing honeyfiles with honeytokens
explain: A honeyfile is a file that alerts when accessed; a honeytoken is traceable data that alerts when used or seen elsewhere.

ask: Which of the following describes a honeytoken?

options.t: A decoy file that alerts when it is opened
options.why: A decoy file that alerts on access is a honeyfile.

options.t: A single decoy system on the network
options.why: A decoy system is a honeypot.

options.t: A set of linked decoy systems
options.why: Linked decoy systems form a honeynet.

options.t: Fake, traceable data with no legitimate use
options.why: A honeytoken is a piece of fake data, such as a credential or address, whose use or sighting reveals a breach.

explain: A honeytoken is fake but traceable data with no legitimate use, so seeing it used or appear anywhere reveals a breach.

ask: Which of the following is a honeytoken designed to reveal?

options.t: That a decoy file was opened
options.why: Reporting that a decoy file was opened is the job of a honeyfile.

options.t: That a decoy server was scanned
options.why: Scans of a decoy server are reported by a honeypot.
A honeytoken is traceable, so its use or sighting shows where the data went.

options.t: How an attacker moved between decoys
options.why: Movement between decoys is shown by a honeynet.

explain: Honeytokens detect data theft and track where data ends up, even outside the network, because the fake data has no legitimate use anywhere.

stem: The privacy officer of an online florist adds a made-up email address to the customer mailing list. Only the florist's own systems ever send mail to it.
ask: Which of the following would show that the mailing list has leaked?

options.t: Staff opening the mailing list file at work
options.why: Staff open the real list as part of their jobs; that is normal use.

options.t: Outsiders sending mail to that inbox
options.why: The address has no legitimate use outside, so mail from anyone else means the list got out.

options.t: A scan of the mail server from the internet
options.why: Scans happen to any internet server and say nothing about the list leaking.

options.t: A drop in the number of subscribers
options.why: People unsubscribe for many reasons; it shows nothing about a leak.

detail: Only the florist's own systems ever send mail to it
explain: A fake email address is a honeytoken: it has no legitimate use, so seeing it used outside reveals a breach and where data went.

stem: A systems administrator at a hospital chain creates a user account with a name like a real admin's. No one ever uses it, and any sign-in attempt with it raises an alert.
ask: Which of the following has the administrator created?

options.why: A fake credential with no legitimate use, watched for any attempt to use it, is a honeytoken.
A honeyfile is a decoy file that alerts when opened; this is an account.
A honeypot is a whole decoy system; this is one fake credential.
A honeynet is a network of decoy systems.

detail: any sign-in attempt with it raises an alert
explain: Fake credentials are a common honeytoken: they have no legitimate use, so any attempt to use one is a high-confidence alert.

stem: A threat intelligence analyst at a card issuer plants a fake card number that looks valid but belongs to no customer. Weeks later the number appears in a list posted on a criminal forum.
ask: Which of the following does this sighting show?

options.t: Data from inside the company has leaked
options.why: The fake number existed only where it was planted, so its appearance shows that data left the issuer.

options.t: An attacker opened a decoy file on a share
options.why: Nothing here is about a file being opened.

options.t: A decoy server was scanned from outside
options.why: Nothing here is about a decoy server.

options.t: A real customer's card was charged
options.why: The number belongs to no customer, so no real card was involved.

detail: the number appears in a list posted on a criminal forum
explain: A honeytoken detects exfiltration: when the planted fake data shows up somewhere, it reveals a breach and where the data went.

stem: The risk officer of a payroll provider wants to learn whether its employee records are ever copied out. The theft might go unnoticed inside and come to light only when the data turns up somewhere else.
ask: Which of the following BEST meets this goal?

options.why: A honeypot catches contact with a decoy system, but not where real data ends up.
Fake records planted among the real ones reveal the theft wherever they turn up.
A honeyfile alerts when it is opened inside, but the theft may go unnoticed inside.
A honeynet shows movement between decoys, not where copied data goes.

detail: come to light only when the data turns up somewhere else
edge: A honeypot also detects intruders, but only when they touch the decoy; the goal is to notice the data turning up elsewhere, which only a honeytoken does.
explain: Honeytokens detect data theft and work even after the data leaves the network, by alerting when the fake data is used or seen.

stem: A database architect at an insurer mixes up tokenization and honeytokens in a design review.
ask: Which of the following describes the difference?

options.t: Honeytokens replace real card numbers to protect them
options.why: Replacing real data with a stand-in to protect it is tokenization.

options.t: Tokenization plants decoys to catch attackers
options.why: Tokenization protects real data; it plants no decoys.

options.t: Honeytokens are fake data planted to detect theft
options.why: A honeytoken is decoy data for detection; tokenization swaps real data for a stand-in to protect it.
Neither is encryption: one is a decoy, the other a substitution.

detail: mixes up tokenization and honeytokens
explain: A honeytoken is not tokenization: tokenization replaces real data for protection, while a honeytoken is fake data planted for detection.

stem: An identity engineer at a software maker receives the alert below. The login named in it was planted in one place only.
ask: Which of the following does this alert show?

lines: planted only in: support bundle sent to vendor 2026-04-02

options.t: A decoy file on a share was opened
options.why: No file was opened; a planted credential was used.

options.t: The VPN gateway itself was compromised
options.why: The gateway refused the login; the leak was of the credential, not the gateway.

options.t: Vendor staff used the bundle's login for support
options.why: A decoy login has no legitimate use, so no one should use it for support.

options.t: The vendor's copy of the bundle was exposed
options.why: The decoy login lived only in the bundle sent to the vendor, so its use traces the leak there.

detail: planted only in: support bundle sent to vendor 2026-04-02
explain: Because each honeytoken is planted in one known place, its use shows which copy of the data was taken.

stem: During a test at a water utility, a red team member finds a credential named "DECOY_DO_NOT_USE" in a configuration file and skips it.
ask: Which change would make this control work?

options.t: Store it in a password-protected file
options.why: Hiding it better does not help if its name gives it away.

options.t: Name it after the security team instead
options.why: A name pointing at the security team is just as easy to skip.

options.t: Use a believable name and format
options.why: A honeytoken works only if an attacker believes it is real.

options.t: Remove its alert so that it stays quiet
options.why: Without an alert the decoy detects nothing at all.

detail: a credential named "DECOY_DO_NOT_USE"
explain: A honeytoken that looks obviously fake will be skipped by a skilled attacker; it must look like a real item.

stem: A deception planner at an online marketplace lists candidate decoys for the coming quarter.
ask: Which of the following candidates are honeytokens? (Select TWO)

options.t: A spreadsheet that alerts when opened
options.why: A decoy file that alerts on access is a honeyfile.

options.t: A fake API key placed in a config file
options.why: A fake key is traceable data with no legitimate use.

options.t: A made-up email address on the mailing list
options.why: A fake address is traceable data that reveals a leak when mail reaches it.

options.t: A decoy server running a fake storefront
options.why: A decoy server is a honeypot.

options.t: A network of fake storefront servers
options.why: A network of decoys is a honeynet.

detail: candidate decoys for the coming quarter
explain: Honeytokens are pieces of fake data: credentials, keys, records or email addresses. Decoy systems, networks and files are the other three kinds.
